About this book. I wrote this as a free, evidence-based companion to the System of Inevitability, which I created. Descriptions of the System's striking methods are drawn from a project document that consolidates a May 2026 conversation about the system, and from an October 2026 viability assessment. Where this book suggests progressions, tests, stop rules, or ethical guidelines, those are my suggestions based on the general scientific literature, not a formal syllabus.

Health and safety notice. This book is for education and inspiration. It is not medical, legal, or self-defence instruction, and it does not replace a physician, physiotherapist, qualified coach, or lawyer. Striking hard objects can fracture the hand and damage the wrist. Striking people can injure, disable, or kill them. Consult a qualified professional before you begin, especially if you have any hand, wrist, elbow, shoulder, heart, bone, or nerve condition. You train at your own risk, and you alone are responsible for how you use what you learn.

About the science. Every study cited here was checked against its published record (authors, year, journal, and DOI) at the time of writing. No study, number, or quotation has been invented. Where the evidence is thin or absent, the text says so.

Dedication

For the ones who could have struck and chose not to.

And for every training partner who trusted someone else’s hands with their face.

How to Read This Book

If you have read Walking and Turning, the first book in this series, you already know the promise this book makes: it will tell you, at every important turn, how sure we are.

That promise matters even more here. The first book was about juggling iron and spinning a ring on a bar. This one is about the hand as a striking tool, the wave of the body behind it, and close-range fighting. That is a subject where myths are everywhere, where confident claims are cheap, and where being wrong can hurt someone. So you will again see three kinds of marked boxes:

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Supported by multiple independent studies, systematic reviews, or meta-analyses with reasonably consistent results, or by basic physics that is not in dispute. You can lean on these.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive or emerging. Supported by real peer-reviewed research, but the studies are few, small, short, indirect, or debated. Promising, but hold them loosely.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner experience and philosophy. Ideas, claims, images, and experiences from the System of Inevitability or from other martial traditions that have not been directly measured. They may be true and useful. They have not been tested.

And the box you should never skip:

⚠ Caution

Caution. Practical safety information. A fist is a small bundle of fragile bones. A head is not designed to be struck. Read these.

Citations appear as author and year, for example (McGill et al., 2010). The full list, with journal details and DOIs, is in the References at the back. A sentence that makes a factual claim with no citation and no box is my reasonable summary or opinion. When this book draws on research already discussed in Book 1, it says so, so that the two books can be read together.

A word about the words. The System of Inevitability describes itself in a rich vocabulary: toroidal energy fields, butterfly-flutter resonance, fractal kinetic chaining, psychological inevitability, a living club. This book honours that vocabulary as what it is: the images a practitioner uses to organize movement and intention. It does not treat those images as physics. Wherever such a phrase appears, the text explains the ordinary, measurable mechanics that may sit underneath it: momentum, angular velocity, effective mass, elastic energy, timing. Where no study has measured a claim, it is labelled untested, however good it sounds.

A word about the phrase “upgrade in human consciousness.” In Book 1 this phrase was treated as an inspirational theme rooted in attention, learning, and flow. In this book it takes on a second, sharper meaning. A person who learns to strike well has acquired a capacity to harm. The upgrade this book cares about is the one that comes with that capacity: more self-control, more awareness, better judgement, and a deeper commitment to never using force when anything else will do. That is not a metaphysical claim. It is an ethical one, and it is the centre of this book.

Foreword

“No instructors required. No belts. Just the tools, the physics, and the will to train.” — from the System of Inevitability project materials

The first book in this series ended with an image of a spiral turning outward: one person practising patiently in a backyard, and that patience spreading to others. This second book begins somewhere harder.

The System of Inevitability is, among other things, a martial system. With iron balls and a spinning ring bar I developed tools for building strong hands, resilient wrists, calm attention, and whole-body coordination. I also developed a way of striking at close range: a hooked, bent-wrist fist borrowed from Southeast Asian Silat; a wave of motion that travels from the ground through the body and out through the knuckles, the hammerfist, the forearm, the elbow, and the shoulder; and a single-arm sequence of strikes that loops in a tight figure-eight and returns to its beginning. The project materials call this sequence a micro-vortex.

When I set out to write a second book, I faced a choice. I could write a manual of hitting, or I could write the kind of book the first one was: an honest companion that takes a practitioner’s ideas seriously, sets them beside the best available peer-reviewed science, marks clearly what is known and what is not, and tries to make the reader wiser as well as more capable.

I chose the second, for three reasons.

The first is honesty. The science of striking is real and fascinating: whip physics, the proximal-to-distal sequencing of throwing and punching, the “double peak” of muscle activation in elite fighters, the effective mass behind a blow, the buttressing structure of the human fist. But almost none of it has been applied to the specific methods of this system. Many of the system’s most striking claims have never been measured. A companion that pretended otherwise would betray the reader.

The second is safety. The hand is a remarkable but fragile structure. Hand and wrist injuries are among the most common injuries in boxing and martial arts. A book that inspired someone to bend their wrist sharply and pound a steel-armed dummy before they were ready would be doing harm.

The third is the reason this series exists at all. I want these books to help ordinary people become more awake, more skilful, and kinder. A striking art can do that. The evidence on martial arts and wellbeing is encouraging, though mixed, and the best evidence suggests that how an art is taught, and what it values, matters enormously. A striking art taught without restraint can make people worse. So this book puts ethics where it belongs: in the middle, not in a footnote.

Read it slowly. Train even more slowly. And if what you learn here ever tempts you toward violence that isn’t strictly necessary, put the book down and walk.

Cory Snell November 2026

Part I · The Hand

A hand that can close into a fist is a hand that can also open.

An Invitation to Restraint

Chapter 1

The strongest hand in the room is the one that does not need to strike.

Make a fist. Slowly.

Notice what happens. Your fingertips curl into your palm and press there. The middle segments of your fingers fold down and lock. Your thumb swings across and clamps over the index and middle fingers. Tendons that run from your forearm through the narrow tunnel of your wrist draw tight. Your forearm hardens. If you pay attention, you may feel your shoulder and even your breath change a little, as if the body as a whole were getting ready for something.

Now open it again, just as slowly.

That small cycle, closing and opening, is the subject of this book. The closing is the obvious part: how a fist is built, how force travels through it, how a wave of motion from the ground can be focused into a few square centimetres of knuckle, forearm, or elbow. The opening is the less obvious part, and the more important one: the relaxation that makes speed possible, the calm that makes good decisions possible under pressure, and the moral choice to keep the hand open whenever you can.

Where this book fits

This is the second book in a series of free, evidence-based companions to the System of Inevitability, emergent, free-form body expression with no set form, developed over more than twenty-five years. It is a conceptual adjective that can be incorporated into any practice, anywhere, by anyone, and it claims no superiority. The first book, Walking and Turning, looked at the system’s conditioning tools: three six-pound iron balls juggled in the Cascade, the Mills Mess, and the Box; a five-foot, twenty-five-pound steel bar carrying a spinning two-pound iron ring; and the philosophy that “training method is just walking and turning.” It set those tools beside the science of brain plasticity, motor learning, tendon and muscle adaptation, flow, and mood.

This book turns to the other half of the system: what the project materials call its close-quarters striking architecture. That includes:

  • the “J” fist, or bent fist, a clenched fist held with the wrist sharply flexed, drawn from the Monyet (“monkey”) hand of Southeast Asian Silat;
  • whole-body wave energy, a pulse of compression and release that travels from the ground or core through the body and is “cycled” through every striking surface: bent knuckles, hammerfist, forearm, elbow, and shoulder;
  • figure-eight, toroidal, and helical geometry as the organizing image of movement;
  • a single-arm micro-vortex: a bent-fist punch, an elbow to the same spot, a backward hammerfist, a lateral elbow, and a return to the punch, all in one tight loop;
  • “rock in a sock” delivery: a relaxed, whip-like swing that locks only at impact;
  • a metal-armed training dummy and a freestanding heavy bag; and
  • breath synchronization, with acknowledged parallels to the Russian art of Systema.

The book takes each of these seriously. For each one, it asks three questions. What does the system claim? What does peer-reviewed science say about the mechanics underneath? And what has not yet been tested, and how could it be?

What this book is not

It is not a fighting manual. It will not teach you to hurt anyone, and it will spend a whole chapter on why, when, and whether you ever should.

It is not an endorsement of every claim in the source material. The materials that describe the system are enthusiastic. They describe a “living geometric engine for close-quarters dominance,” energy economy “approaching 100%,” a fist that is “structurally superior” to the conventional one, and “4–5 stacked impacts in under one second.” Some of these may turn out to be partly true. None of them has been measured. This book will say so each time, and then suggest how someone could find out.

It is not the last word. The science of striking is young, and the science of this particular system does not yet exist. The project’s own viability assessment of October 2026 judged the method conditionally viable as personal conditioning and not yet viable as a fully transmissible system until it has progressions, filmed standards, and outcome data. That is an honest place to begin, and it is where this book begins.

An untested claim is not a false claim. It is an invitation to test.

The two kinds of strength

A striking art builds two kinds of strength at once, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is the strength to act: fast hands, a sturdy wrist, a body that moves as one piece, the ability to produce a sharp, heavy impact at close range. Most of this book’s science is about that kind of strength, because that is where the research is: in biomechanics, motor learning, and exercise physiology.

The second is the strength to refrain: to notice fear and anger without being driven by them, to read a situation accurately, to choose the least harmful option, to walk away, and to protect the people who train with you. This kind of strength is harder to measure, but it is not beyond science. There is real research on how martial arts training relates to aggression and wellbeing, on how people perform under stress, on de-escalation, and on the attention and self-regulation that mindfulness and breath training can build. That research is mixed in places, and this book reports the mixture honestly. But one thread runs through it clearly: what a training culture values seems to matter as much as what it trains.

The phrase that inspires this series is “an upgrade in human consciousness.” In a book about striking, this book can give that phrase only one honest meaning. It is the upgrade from being able to hurt to being trustworthy with that ability.

How the book is arranged

Part I, The Hand, introduces the system’s striking ideas as the project materials describe them (Chapter 2), and then looks closely at the bent fist: what anatomy and biomechanics say about wrist position, grip, the buttressed fist, and hand injury (Chapter 3).

Part II, The Wave, explores the physics and physiology of whole-body striking: the whip and the kinetic chain (Chapter 4), relaxation, stiffness, and effective mass (Chapter 5), the figure-eight micro-vortex and how coordination patterns switch (Chapter 6), and breath (Chapter 7).

Part III, The Learning, turns to how such skills are learned: the science of variable, “non-repetitive” practice (Chapter 8), perception and timing against a living opponent (Chapter 9), and calm under pressure (Chapter 10).

Part IV, The Responsibility, holds the most important chapters: the ethics of the closed hand (Chapter 11), a suggested safe progression for the bent fist and the micro-vortex (Chapter 12), and a practical guide to testing the system’s claims honestly (Chapter 13). A short closing chapter, test protocols, an evidence summary, a glossary, and full references follow.

If you read only three chapters, read 11, 12, and 13.

⚠ Caution

Before you try anything in this book: striking hard surfaces with a bent wrist is a recognized way to injure the hand and wrist. Chapter 12 gives a conservative, staged progression and stop rules. Do not skip to the metal-armed dummy.

The Shape of the System

Chapter 2

Defense and offense are indistinguishable; energy is recycled internally. — from the System of Inevitability project materials

Before testing any idea, it is only fair to state it as its holder would. This chapter describes the System of Inevitability’s close-range striking ideas as they appear in the project materials, a consolidation of a detailed conversation about the system held in May 2026. Analysis and evidence come in later chapters. Here, the aim is to listen.

A system of flow, not of techniques

The project materials describe the System of Inevitability as a solitary, principle-based martial synthesis optimized for close-quarters combat, the range from zero to about two feet, sometimes called infighting. Rather than a catalogue of separate techniques, it treats combat as “continuous, self-sustaining flow.”

Its stated foundations are:

  • natural biomechanics and everyday human movement, with “no exotic stances”;
  • applied geometry, especially figure-eight infinity loops, toroidal (doughnut-shaped) energy fields, and helical spirals;
  • fluid-dynamic images: “butterfly-flutter micro-vibrations,” vortices, and wave propagation;
  • non-repetitive, fractal kinetic chaining, meaning that combinations are not memorized but generated afresh from underlying patterns; and
  • influences from Silat (the Monyet or “J” hand), from Systema-style wave and relaxation principles, and from what the materials call predatory archetypes.

The intended result is that defence and offence become indistinguishable, energy is “recycled internally,” and the practitioner “imposes geometry on the opponent rather than meeting force with force.” The name of the system comes from a feeling this is meant to produce: outcomes that seem inevitable because they emerge from universal patterns rather than from memorized forms.

The “J” fist

The signature tool is the “J” fist, or bent fist. It is a clenched fist held with extreme palmar flexion: the wrist bent sharply downward toward the palm, so that hand and forearm form a hook, like a candy cane or the letter J. The materials link it to the Tangan Monyet, the monkey hand, of Silat lineages such as Cimande and Serak.

In this position, the materials say, the pinky edge of the fist, the ulnar border of the forearm (the side on the little-finger side), and the elbow form a single continuous striking surface, a “living club.” The wrist lock is said to align the bones for force transmission and protect against hyperextension. The same structure can hammer, chop, slash, hook, and trap, and at close range it allows control of an opponent’s arm or neck at the same time as striking.

The materials go further and argue that the bent fist is superior to a conventional straight fist for close-quarters work, for four reasons: structural integrity under misaligned impact; better “wave transmission” through a short lever and whip-like swing; seamless chaining between fist, hammerfist, forearm, and elbow without resetting; and compactness in entanglement. The straight fist, on this view, is optimized for longer range and discrete strikes.

The wave

At the centre of the system is whole-body wave energy: a helical pulse of compression and release that originates from the ground or core, travels through the kinetic chain, and then recycles. At close range the wave “collapses into micro-waves.”

The wave can be cycled through every striking surface in turn: the bent knuckles, the hammerfist, the forearm, the elbow, and the shoulder. On a freestanding heavy bag, from a stationary rooted position, these surfaces string together “like alternating juggling patterns.” The practitioner does not pre-plan the sequence. The geometry and the feedback from the bag generate the patterns on the fly.

Readers of Walking and Turning will recognize the family resemblance. The juggling patterns of Book 1 (the cascade, the Mills Mess, the Box) are cycles in which each hand’s action creates the conditions for the next. The system’s striking work is described in the same terms: not a list of strikes, but a pattern that keeps itself going.

The micro-vortex

The materials describe one specific sequence in detail, which they call the single-arm micro-vortex. It uses one hand and elbow, moving in small circular pathways of about 8 to 14 inches:

  1. A straight bent-fist punch, delivered with a relaxed, whipping “rock in a sock” swing that locks into the J shape only at impact.
  2. A same-spot elbow: the hand opens, the wrist snaps into extreme flexion, and the elbow springs outward and upward to strike the exact point the fist just hit.
  3. A backward hammerfist: the elbow’s rebound reverses the momentum into a backward or diagonal hammerfist, again with a whipping quality.
  4. A lateral elbow: the momentum switches again into a tight sideways elbow snap.
  5. A natural return to the straight punch, and the cycle restarts.

One continuous helical wave is said to power the whole cycle. The momentum switches trace “an oscillating toroidal figure-8 within the small circle,” and the J-shaped wrist acts as a “universal adapter” between surfaces. The materials describe the result as “4–5 stacked impacts in under one second” on or near the same target, “with compounding resonance and no resets,” and say the sequence feels automatic once the wave is initiated. It is trained from a stationary, rooted position.

Tools and training

Two tools carry this part of the system:

  • a wooden training dummy with Schedule 40 steel-pipe arms, built on the pattern of the Wing Chun mook yan jong, providing “hard, unyielding feedback” for alignment, wrist lock, rebound, and conditioning of the striking surfaces; and
  • a freestanding heavy bag, worked from a stationary rooted position, whose rebound assists the momentum switches and builds endurance and instinctive adaptation.

The suggested progression in the materials is slow wave → single-arm vortex → full multi-limb “juggling,” with breath synchronized to the movement: inhale on compression, exhale on release.

Systema as a parallel path

The materials present Russian Systema as a “parallel path up the same mountain.” Both are described as emphasizing non-repetitive flow, natural movement, wave and relaxation principles, and energy recycling. Systema is characterized as breath- and relaxation-centred; Inevitability as more explicitly geometric, with compact J-hand tools for short-range work. Each is said to be able to enrich the other.

A note on ratings

The source conversation also includes numerical ratings: the dummy setup at 9.2 out of 10, the system as a concept at 9.4 and later 9.6, and a 9.1 comparison with elite military close-quarters systems. These numbers came from a conversation with an AI system. They are impressions, not measurements. No one tested anything to produce them, and they are not evidence that the system works, or that it doesn’t. This book mentions them once, here, for completeness, and does not rely on them. Chapter 13 explains what real evidence would look like.

To its credit, the same conversation noted that full viability “requires progressive pressure-testing, filmed standards, and outcome data.” That is exactly right, and it is where Part IV of this book will take us.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

What this chapter contains. Everything above is the system’s own description of itself, from its project materials. None of it is a scientific finding. The rest of this book asks, claim by claim, what science can say about it.

The Bent Fist

Chapter 3

A fist is a structure. Structures have strengths, and they have limits.

The human hand has 27 bones, more than a dozen joints in the fingers alone, and tendons that run from muscles in the forearm across the wrist to every finger. It evolved, as far as anyone can tell, mostly for manipulation: gripping, carrying, shaping, throwing, making. It can also be folded into a fist. What happens to a fist when it strikes something is a question that biomechanics, hand surgery, and even evolutionary biology have studied. This chapter gathers what they have found and sets it beside the System of Inevitability’s signature hand, the bent or “J” fist.

How a fist holds together

When you close a conventional fist, the tips of the four fingers press into the palm, the middle segments fold down, and the thumb wraps across the index and middle fingers. The anatomists Michael Morgan and David Carrier called this arrangement buttressing: each part props up the others so that the whole fist behaves less like a bundle of separate bones and more like a single block.

They tested it. In one set of measurements, the buttressed fist made the second knuckle joint about four times stiffer than an unbuttressed one, and force transfer through the thumb more than doubled the ability of the finger bones to transmit punching force. Interestingly, in the same study, peak forces from maximum-effort strikes did not differ between the closed fist and the open palm (Morgan & Carrier, 2013). A follow-up experiment on cadaver arms measured strain in the metacarpal bones (the long bones of the palm) during strikes. Strains were significantly higher with an unbuttressed fist or an open-hand slap. The authors estimated that a person could safely strike with about 55% more force with a fully buttressed fist than with an unbuttressed one, and about twice as much as with an open-handed slap (Horns et al., 2015).

Morgan and Carrier went on to argue that the human hand’s proportions evolved partly for fighting. That evolutionary interpretation has been challenged by other scientists, who point out that a useful feature is not proof that it was selected for that use (Nickle & Goncharoff, 2013). For our purposes, the mechanical findings matter more than the evolutionary story, and they are clear: how the fist is formed changes how well its bones are protected.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Fist structure protects the hand. Laboratory and cadaver studies show that a tightly buttressed fist stiffens the knuckle joints and reduces strain in the metacarpal bones compared with loose or open-hand positions (Morgan & Carrier, 2013; Horns et al., 2015). These are small studies under laboratory conditions; the evolutionary interpretation is debated (Nickle & Goncharoff, 2013). None of these studies tested a bent-wrist fist.

What the wrist does

The fist is only half the structure. Every force that lands on the knuckles must pass through the wrist into the forearm, and the wrist is a complicated joint: two rows of small carpal bones, a web of ligaments, and, on the little-finger side, a cartilage cushion between the forearm’s ulna and the carpals.

Two well-studied facts about the wrist bear directly on the bent fist.

First, wrist position strongly affects grip strength. When people squeeze as hard as they can, they naturally settle into about 35 degrees of wrist extension (bent backward) and slight ulnar deviation (toward the little finger). In a classic study, grip strength was significantly lower in any position that deviated from this self-selected one, and a minimum of about 25 degrees of extension was needed for optimum grip (O’Driscoll et al., 1992). Earlier work had likewise studied how sideways deviation of the wrist affects maximum power grip (Pryce, 1980). The reason is well known to anatomists: the long finger flexor muscles cross the wrist, and when the wrist is flexed they are shortened and slack, so they cannot pull as hard on the fingers.

The J fist places the wrist in extreme flexion, the opposite direction from the strongest grip. No study has measured grip strength or fist integrity in that exact posture, but the direction of the effect is not in doubt: flexing the wrist weakens the clench. A fist that clenches less tightly is, according to the buttressing research above, a fist whose bones are less well protected.

Second, wrist position affects the pressure inside the carpal tunnel, the narrow passage through which the finger tendons and the median nerve run. In a study that measured carpal-tunnel pressure continuously as people moved their wrists, the lowest pressure was found near neutral: on average about 2 degrees of extension and 2 degrees of ulnar deviation (Weiss et al., 1995). Holding the wrist far from neutral raises the pressure on the structures inside.

● Evidence: well-established

Wrist position matters. Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist moderately extended and drops when the wrist moves away from that position, including into flexion (O’Driscoll et al., 1992). Carpal-tunnel pressure is lowest near neutral (Weiss et al., 1995).

What does that mean for the J fist? Not that it is useless, but that its value cannot come from maximum grip. If it has advantages, they must come from somewhere else: from changing which surface lands, from aligning the forearm bones behind a different contact point, from making transitions to the hammerfist and elbow quicker, or from protecting the wrist from being bent backward on impact, which is a real mechanism of injury in punching. Those are interesting hypotheses. They are hypotheses.

Surfaces and pressure

The project materials describe the J fist as turning the pinky edge of the fist, the ulnar border of the forearm, and the elbow into one continuous “living club.” It is a vivid image, and it points to something physical: different surfaces of the arm have very different areas, and the same force spread over a smaller area produces higher pressure.

One study scanned the contact areas of the fist, the palm, and the elbow in 76 adults in striking positions. In both men and women, the palm had the largest contact area and the elbow the smallest (Beranek et al., 2022). A study of trained self-defence practitioners striking a force plate from a dominant ground position found that palm strikes and elbow strikes produced higher peak forces than straight punches, and estimated that men could exceed a force associated with skull fracture with a substantial probability using elbows and palms in that position (Beranek et al., 2020). A forensic study of 50 ordinary volunteers compared the fist, the little-finger edge of the hand (a “karate chop”), and the open hand, and found that the forces depended on technique, sex, hand, and body weight, with large differences between individuals (Adamec et al., 2021).

These studies were not about the J fist. But they support two sober observations. Short, compact strikes with the hard, narrow surfaces of the forearm and elbow can be very forceful. And because those surfaces are small and hard, they concentrate pressure on whatever they hit, which is one reason elbow strikes are restricted or banned in many combat sports. Chapter 11 returns to what that means ethically.

The hand that breaks

the most important fact about the fist for anyone who trains it is this: in elite amateur boxing, the hand is the most commonly injured part of the body.

In five years of medical surveillance of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad, more injuries affected the hand than any other location, in both training and competition (Loosemore et al., 2015). A longer study of the same programme found that instability of the finger joints at the base of the hand and “boxer’s knuckle,” an injury to the tissues over the knuckle, were the most common hand and wrist diagnoses (Loosemore et al., 2017). These were elite athletes, with expert coaching, hand wraps, and gloves.

Outside the ring, the classic hand injury from punching is the boxer’s fracture, a break of the neck of the fifth metacarpal, the bone behind the little-finger knuckle, caused by direct trauma to a clenched fist (Hussain et al., 2020). In the United States, metacarpal fractures are most common in young men, and the most common mechanisms are contact with a wall or door, and falls (Nakashian et al., 2012). The fifth metacarpal is exactly the bone that sits behind the “pinky edge” of the fist that the J fist emphasizes.

In a survey of martial artists, the hand and wrist were the most commonly injured region of the upper body, fractures and dislocations were frequently reported, and hand protection was associated with a lower risk of hand injury (Diesselhorst et al., 2013). A review of hand and wrist injuries in boxing and martial arts concluded that axial loading of the fist causes fractures and dislocations in striking arts, that hand protection clearly reduces risk, and that training in proper technique and target selection is an important part of prevention (Drury et al., 2017).

● Evidence: well-established

Hands break. Hand and wrist injuries are the most common injuries in boxing, even at elite level, and are common in martial arts. Hand protection and good technique reduce the risk (Loosemore et al., 2015, 2017; Diesselhorst et al., 2013; Drury et al., 2017).

⚠ Caution

The bent fist is untested for injury risk. No published study has examined injuries from striking with a sharply flexed wrist. Until such evidence exists, treat the J fist as a higher-risk position for the wrist, not a protective one, and follow the progression in Chapter 12: no hard targets until the wrist has been conditioned for months, light contact first, and immediate stopping at any sharp pain, swelling, numbness, or knuckle that looks or feels different.

The monkey hand and its lineage

The project materials trace the J fist to the Tangan Monyet, the monkey hand of Silat, the family of Southeast Asian martial arts practised across Indonesia, Malaysia, and the wider Malay world. Silat is a rich subject of scholarship in anthropology and ethnomusicology. An edited academic volume has examined pencak silat’s history, standardization, and the music that traditionally accompanies it (Paetzold & Mason, 2016). An anthropological study of Sundanese pencak silat in West Java described how students learn to improvise by mastering generic principles from which “potentially unbounded repertoires” of responses are generated, and contrasted this with nationally standardized, more fixed forms (Wilson, 2009). That observation will matter again in Chapter 8, because it describes, in a scholarly setting, exactly the kind of principle-based, non-repetitive learning the System of Inevitability claims for itself.

This book could find no peer-reviewed biomechanical study of the monkey hand or of any bent-wrist striking posture. The lineage claims in the materials (Cimande, Serak) are the system’s own account of its influences, and they are offered here as that.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

The J fist’s claimed advantages are untested. The claims that the bent fist is “structurally superior” to the straight fist, that its wrist lock “aligns bones for force transmission,” and that it is ideal for continuous close-range chaining come from the system’s own materials. They are plausible as hypotheses about transitions and surfaces. They are in tension with what is known about wrist position and grip. They have not been measured. Chapter 13 suggests how to measure them.

A fair summary

The bent fist is not obviously wrong. Martial traditions all over the world use strikes with the edge of the hand, the forearm, the back of the wrist, and the elbow, and several of those surfaces are forceful at close range. A hand shape that makes it easy to flow between them could genuinely help a practitioner who trains that way.

But “superior” is a strong word, and the evidence we do have points to real costs: a flexed wrist weakens the grip that buttresses the fist, raises pressure in the carpal tunnel, and leaves the vulnerable fifth metacarpal in the front line. If the J fist is to earn its place, it will have to do so in tests that compare it honestly with the conventional fist, on the same target, with the same person, filmed and measured. Until then, the best word for it is not superior or inferior, but interesting.

Part II · The Wave

Ground to hip, hip to shoulder, shoulder to hand. A wave that begins far from where it lands.

The Whip and the Wave

Chapter 4

A wave that can be cycled endlessly through every striking surface. — from the System of Inevitability project materials

Crack a towel. If you have ever done it, you know the trick is not to swing hard with the hand. It is to move the hand sharply and then stop it, letting the motion run down the length of the towel faster and faster until the tip snaps. The hand starts the wave. The towel finishes it.

The System of Inevitability describes its striking power in the language of waves: a “helical compression-release pulse” that begins in the ground or core, travels through the body, and is delivered through the knuckles, hammerfist, forearm, elbow, or shoulder. The materials describe the arm in the strike as “rock in a sock”: relaxed and flail-like during the swing, locking only at impact. This chapter looks at what physics and biomechanics know about exactly this kind of motion, because, as it happens, they know quite a lot.

The proximal-to-distal sequence

Watch a baseball pitcher, a tennis server, a javelin thrower, or a boxer throwing a long punch in slow motion, and you will see a pattern. The big, heavy segments near the centre of the body start moving first: the legs push, the hips rotate, then the trunk. The lighter segments farther out (the upper arm, the forearm, the hand) start later, but reach higher speeds. Each segment seems to hand its motion on to the next.

Biomechanists call this proximal-to-distal sequencing, and it is one of the most consistent findings in the science of throwing, kicking, and striking. A classic review showed that the motions of body segments in these skills are generally sequenced from the centre outward, and explained why: the segments are linked, so the motion of one segment produces forces on the next. When the upper arm accelerates forward, the forearm at first lags behind; then, as the upper arm’s motion interacts with the forearm, the forearm whips forward, and its motion in turn slows the upper arm (Putnam, 1993). These “motion-dependent” interactions mean that a well-timed sequence lets the outer segments move faster than the muscles acting on them alone could make them move.

A study of skilled baseball players made the point in a striking way. Using a method that separates the torque a muscle produces at a joint from the torque transmitted to it by the motion of other segments, it found that throwers generated large angular velocities at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist largely by exploiting these interaction torques. To throw faster, they increased muscle torque at the trunk and shoulder, but not at the elbow and wrist. The proximal muscles created “a dynamic foundation” for the whole limb (Hirashima et al., 2007).

The traditional picture has also been refined. A review of the tennis serve and squash forehand showed that twisting rotations along the long axis of the upper arm and forearm reach their peak speeds late in the stroke and are essential to racquet speed. Simple “centre-outward” sequencing was not enough to describe what was happening (Marshall & Elliott, 2000). The body’s chain is not just a chain of hinges; it is a chain of spirals.

In an analysis of the overarm throw in 56 handball players, nearly three quarters of the work done on the ball was done in the last 50 milliseconds of the throw, and the authors described a “flow of energy from proximal to distal segments” (Jöris et al., 1985).

● Evidence: well-established

The kinetic chain is real. In throwing, kicking, and striking, body segments are generally sequenced from proximal to distal, and skilled performers use the mechanical interaction between linked segments to generate high speeds at the hand. Long-axis rotations of the arm add to this (Putnam, 1993; Hirashima et al., 2007; Marshall & Elliott, 2000; Jöris et al., 1985).

Does this apply to punching? Partly. A punch is not a throw: the hand doesn’t let go, and the goal is usually force on a target rather than maximum speed at release. But studies that have mapped the phases of boxing punches with force plates, muscle recordings, and high-speed video describe a similar flow from the ground through the hips and trunk to the arm (Lenetsky et al., 2020). A classic kinematic analysis of boxing punches likewise examined how the upper limb segments move during different punches (Whiting et al., 1988), and a review of the contributors to punching force highlights the role of ground reaction forces, the push of the feet against the floor (Lenetsky et al., 2013). The system’s image of a wave that begins “from the ground or core” is, in this sense, describing something real.

Whips, sockets, and rocks

Why does a whip crack? The answer has been worked out by applied mathematicians. A wave started at the handle travels down the whip, and because the whip tapers and is under tension, the wave speeds up as it travels, until the tip moves faster than sound and produces a small sonic boom (Goriely & McMillen, 2002; McMillen & Goriely, 2003). The handle never moves anywhere near that fast. The speed is produced by the shape and flexibility of the system, not by the force at the handle alone.

The human arm is not a whip. It is a chain of a few rigid segments with joints, not a flexible tapered cord. But it shares an essential feature: energy put in at the heavy end can be transferred to the light end and concentrated there, if the timing is right. Engineers have long modelled the golf swing, for example, as a double pendulum: two linked rods, the arms and the club, where a well-timed release of the wrist lets the clubhead overtake the hands (Pickering & Vickers, 1999).

“Rock in a sock” is a vivid name for exactly this: a heavy object at the end of a flexible link. In the micro-vortex, the “sock” is a relaxed forearm and wrist, and the “rock” is the fist or the forearm itself. If the wrist and elbow stay loose during the swing, the hand can lag behind and then whip through, picking up speed from the motion of the shoulder and upper arm, just as the forearm does in a throw.

Springs in the body

There is a second source of “wave energy” that the body has and a towel does not: elastic recoil. Tendons and other connective tissues can store energy when they are stretched and return much of it when they recoil. The body uses these biological springs in running, jumping, and throwing (Roberts & Azizi, 2011). When a muscle is actively stretched just before it shortens, a pattern called the stretch-shortening cycle, it can produce more force and power than it would from a standing start (Komi, 2000).

The most dramatic example is throwing. Experiments with human throwers showed that our ability to throw fast depends on several anatomical features that let the shoulder store elastic energy as the arm is cocked back and release it as the arm whips forward. Those features appear together in the fossil record about two million years ago (Roach et al., 2013).

The project materials describe the wave as “compression-release.” That is not a bad informal description of a stretch-shortening cycle: a loading phase in which tissues are tensioned, followed by a release in which they recoil. Whether the specific movements of the micro-vortex use elastic recoil efficiently has never been studied. But the general principle that a body can store energy in a “wind-up” and return it in a “release” is solid.

● Evidence: well-established

The body stores and returns elastic energy. Tendons and connective tissue act as springs; the stretch-shortening cycle enhances force and power; human throwing relies on elastic energy storage at the shoulder (Roberts & Azizi, 2011; Komi, 2000; Roach et al., 2013).

What “wave energy” really means

It is worth slowing down here, because words matter.

In physics, a wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another. A wave through the human body during a strike is a reasonable metaphor for what the kinetic-chain research describes: motion that starts in one place and arrives, amplified in speed, somewhere else. The underlying quantities are ordinary ones:

  • momentum, the product of mass and velocity, which is what a strike delivers to a target;
  • angular velocity, how fast each segment rotates, which is what the sequencing research measures;
  • interaction torques, by which one moving segment drives the next;
  • elastic energy, stored and released by tendons and connective tissue; and
  • effective mass, how much of the body’s mass is effectively “behind” the strike at impact (the subject of the next chapter).

None of these involve a “field.” A toroid is a doughnut shape, and a path that loops around and returns, like the micro-vortex, can certainly trace something like a doughnut in space. That is geometry, and it may be a useful image for organizing practice. But there is no evidence that a human body generates a “toroidal energy field,” and nothing in biomechanics requires one to explain how strikes work.

The same is true of “butterfly-flutter resonance” and “penetrating micro-vibrations.” Resonance is a real phenomenon in physics: a system driven at its natural frequency oscillates with growing amplitude. But no study has shown that striking with a relaxed arm produces resonance in a target, or that micro-vibrations add meaningfully to the damage of an impact. In ordinary collision mechanics, the important quantities are the momentum delivered and how quickly it is delivered (Walker, 1975; Wilk et al., 1983). If the system’s “flutter” corresponds to anything measurable, a high-speed camera and a force sensor could find it. Until then, it is an image.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Toroidal fields, flutter, and resonance are metaphors. The project materials’ descriptions of “toroidal energy fields,” “butterfly-flutter resonance,” and “fractal” chaining are practitioner imagery. They may help organize movement and attention. They are not supported by physics or biomechanics research, which explains striking with momentum, angular velocity, interaction torques, elastic energy, and effective mass.

The physics underneath is wonderful enough. It does not need to be dressed up.

The wave, honestly told

Here, then, is what we can say with confidence. Skilled striking and throwing do use something like a wave: a timed sequence of segment motions from the centre of the body outward, exploiting the mechanical coupling between segments and the elasticity of tissues, so that the hand or elbow moves faster than the muscles acting on it could achieve alone. Relaxation of the outer segments during the swing is likely to help this, because a stiff, braced arm cannot be whipped. That is a real foundation for the system’s wave.

And here is what we cannot yet say: whether the specific micro-movements of the System of Inevitability produce an efficient kinetic chain; whether a wave can be “cycled endlessly” through successive surfaces without losing most of its energy each time; and whether the system’s strikes are faster, heavier, or more efficient than conventional ones. Those are questions for a camera, a force sensor, and patience.

Loose Until It Lands

Chapter 5

Relaxed during the arc; locked at impact. — the “rock in a sock” principle, from the project materials

There is a paradox at the heart of striking, and a group of researchers led by the spine biomechanist Stuart McGill put it plainly. When a muscle contracts, it produces force, which creates movement. But it also becomes stiffer, and stiffness resists rapid changes of shape and slows the joint down. Force makes you fast; stiffness makes you slow. How, then, does a fighter produce a strike that is both very fast and very heavy?

The double peak

To find out, McGill and colleagues recorded the muscle activity and spine motion of five elite mixed martial arts fighters as they struck a heavy bag (McGill et al., 2010). In many of the strikes, the muscles showed not one burst of activity but two, a double peak:

  1. A first peak at the very start of the movement, which the authors suggested stiffens the body’s core and creates a stable base, “an inertial mass” for the limbs to “pry” against as they begin to move.
  2. A phase of relaxation, in which some muscles switched off as the limb sped up.
  3. A second peak at the moment of contact with the bag, which the authors proposed stiffens the whole body linkage, increasing the effective mass behind the strike and likely its force.

The authors described this as a “contract–relax–contract” pulse and suggested that training should pay attention not only to how fast a muscle can switch on but to how fast it can switch off.

Read that description again with “rock in a sock” in mind: a relaxed, flail-like swing that locks only at impact. The System of Inevitability’s principle and the double-peak pattern are strikingly similar. The system arrived at it through practice; the researchers found it in elite fighters with electrodes. This is one of the most encouraging points of contact between the system and the science.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Relax to accelerate, stiffen to strike. Elite fighters show a double peak of muscle activation, with relaxation between an initial stiffening and a second burst at impact (McGill et al., 2010). The study was small (five athletes) and descriptive; the proposed functions of each peak are reasonable interpretations, not direct measurements. The pattern closely resembles the system’s “rock in a sock” principle.

Effective mass

When a fist strikes a target, how much of the body is “behind” it? Not the whole body: the arm is linked to the trunk by soft, moving joints. But not just the fist either. Biomechanists use the idea of effective mass: the mass that, moving at the speed of the hand, would deliver the same momentum to the target. A loose arm behaves like a light object; a stiffened, well-aligned arm and trunk behave like a heavier one.

The idea has been tested directly. In a study of palm strikes against a basketball, kung fu practitioners struck with greater hand speed than non-practitioners (about 6.7 versus 5.0 metres per second), but the larger difference was in effective mass, about 2.6 kilograms versus 1.3. For untrained people, the effective mass was statistically the same as the mass of their hand and forearm; for the martial artists, it was significantly greater. The authors suggested that against heavier targets, effective mass might be the main factor distinguishing trained from untrained strikers (Neto et al., 2007).

In a study of Olympic boxers punching an instrumented crash-test dummy head, straight punches averaged about 3,400 newtons of force at hand speeds around 9 metres per second, with an average effective punch mass of about 2.9 kilograms. Heavier boxers hit harder, mainly because their effective mass was larger (Walilko et al., 2005). A review of effective mass in combat sports concluded that it is a useful measure but that punching complicates it, because the puncher continues to push during the impact (Lenetsky et al., 2015). Using a purpose-built boxing dynamometer, another study found that elite boxers’ rear-hand straight punches averaged about 4,800 newtons, compared with about 2,400 for novices (Smith et al., 2000).

Physicists, too, have long been interested in striking. Analyses of the karate punch as collision mechanics showed that damage to a target depends on contact being made when the fist is moving fastest, and that “focusing” a punch to finish a few centimetres inside the target maximizes deformation (Walker, 1975). Later work examined the dynamics and biomechanics of karate strikes in more detail (Wilk et al., 1983).

● Evidence: well-established

Speed and effective mass both matter. The impact of a strike depends on the speed of the striking segment and on how much mass is effectively coupled behind it at contact. Trained strikers tend to have higher effective mass than untrained ones (Neto et al., 2007; Walilko et al., 2005; Lenetsky et al., 2015).

What the research suggests for “rock in a sock”

Put together, the double-peak findings and the effective-mass findings tell a coherent story that fits the system’s principle well:

  • A relaxed swing allows the distal segments to whip through faster, exploiting the kinetic chain described in Chapter 4.
  • A stiffening at impact couples more of the body’s mass behind the contact point, increasing effective mass.
  • Timing is everything: stiffening too early slows the strike; stiffening too late lets the hand “bounce” off, delivering little momentum and risking injury to a loose wrist.

That last point deserves emphasis. A loose wrist at the moment of impact is a classic way to sprain or fracture the hand. The “lock at impact” part of “rock in a sock” is not optional. It is what protects the hand, and it is a skill that has to be learned gradually, at low force, before any hard target is struck.

Palms, elbows, and the variety of strikes

The project materials describe a whole family of strikes: bent-knuckle punches, hammerfists, forearm strikes, elbows, and shoulders. What does research say about how they compare?

The best overview is a systematic review and meta-analysis of upper-limb strikes in combat sports. It found 28 studies covering nine kinds of strike. Straight punches and reverse punches produced larger mean impact forces than a kung fu punch, and palm strikes were slower than several kinds of punch. The highest mean force recorded in the literature was for a straight punch, about 3,400 newtons (Beránek et al., 2023). The review’s authors noted that relatively few strike types have been studied.

As Chapter 3 described, a later study of trained practitioners striking from a dominant position on the ground found that palm strikes and elbow strikes produced higher peak forces than straight punches in that position (Beranek et al., 2020). Elbow strikes also have the smallest contact area of the common striking surfaces (Beranek et al., 2022). Forensic measurements of fist, hand-edge, and open-hand strikes in ordinary volunteers showed large differences between individuals (Adamec et al., 2021). And in hand-dominance studies of kung fu palm strikes, strikes were stronger with the dominant hand and when stepping toward the target (Neto et al., 2012).

What has not been studied, as far as this book could find:

  • the bent-knuckle J-fist punch;
  • the backward hammerfist;
  • strikes delivered in rapid succession by the same arm on the same spot;
  • the force of a strike that begins from the rebound of the previous one.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“100% energy economy” and “zero wasted motion” are untested. The project materials describe the system as approaching 100% energy economy. No human movement does this. Muscles convert chemical energy to mechanical work with substantial losses as heat; each impact dissipates energy into the target and into the striker’s own tissues; and every change of direction costs energy. These phrases are best read as an aspiration toward economy of motion, which can be studied (Chapter 13), not as a measurable claim.

Does the wave “recycle”?

The micro-vortex is described as recycling energy: the rebound of one strike powering the next. There is a real physical idea in here. When a fist or elbow hits a heavy bag and bounces back, some of the kinetic energy returns as rebound motion. A skilled practitioner could redirect that rebound into the next movement instead of stopping it and starting over. In elastic tissues, too, energy stored during a deceleration can be partly returned in the next acceleration (Roberts & Azizi, 2011).

But physics sets limits. Every impact that deforms a target converts much of the strike’s energy into deformation, heat, and sound. That is, after all, what a strike is for. The energy that comes back from a heavy bag is a fraction of what went in, and the energy that comes back from a person is less, and less predictable. A sequence of strikes can be made efficient, by avoiding pauses and wasted movement, but it cannot be self-powering. Each strike in the micro-vortex still has to be driven by the body’s muscles. A good way to think of “recycling” is as the skill of not wasting the rebound, rather than as a source of free energy.

Efficiency is not the absence of effort. It is effort that arrives where it is needed and nowhere else.

Training the switch

If relaxation is a skill, how is it trained? Here the research is thin. McGill and colleagues suggested “pulse training” that emphasizes the rate of relaxation as well as contraction (McGill et al., 2010), but did not test it. One study of runners found that consciously relaxing the hands and upper body did not improve running economy, while periodic smiling did, slightly (Brick et al., 2018). That is a reminder that “relax” is a hard instruction to follow on purpose, and that indirect cues sometimes work better than direct ones.

The system’s own approach, slow wave practice before speed, single-arm sequences before multi-limb ones, and a freestanding bag that gives honest feedback, is a reasonable way to explore the skill. The safe progression in Chapter 12 builds on it: slow, unloaded movement first, then light contact, then gradually increasing speed and force, always with the “lock at impact” in place before power is added.

Figure-Eights and Momentum Switches

Chapter 6

Momentum switches create an oscillating figure-8 within the small circle. — from the System of Inevitability project materials

Readers of Walking and Turning met the figure-eight before. The three-ball cascade, the first juggling pattern, traces a sideways figure-eight in the air as the balls cross from hand to hand. Researchers who studied cascade juggling found that skilled jugglers are not rigid metronomes but flexibly coupled oscillators, adjusting the timing of each hand to keep the whole pattern stable (Beek & Turvey, 1992). The figure-eight, in juggling, is not a shape anyone draws on purpose. It emerges from the rules of the pattern.

The System of Inevitability uses the same image for its close-range striking. Its single-arm micro-vortex (punch, same-spot elbow, backward hammerfist, lateral elbow, return) is said to trace an oscillating figure-eight within a small circle, with momentum “switching” at each transition. This chapter asks what science can say about patterns like this: how they hold together, how they switch, and how they come to feel automatic.

Patterns that organize themselves

In the 1980s, the physicist Hermann Haken and the neuroscientist Scott Kelso, with Herbert Bunz, published a mathematical model of a deceptively simple experiment. In earlier experiments by Kelso, people moved their two hands or index fingers back and forth, either in mirror symmetry (in phase) or in parallel (anti-phase), and to speed up gradually. People who started in the anti-phase pattern, past a certain speed, spontaneously switched to the in-phase pattern, without meaning to. The reverse did not happen. The model, now known as the HKB model, explained this as a phase transition in a self-organizing system: as a control parameter (speed) changed, one stable pattern of coordination lost its stability and the system jumped to another (Haken et al., 1985). Kelso and Schöner went on to develop this into a general account of how coordinated movement patterns self-organize (Kelso & Schöner, 1988).

The same kind of dynamics has been found in real fighting. In a study of expert kendo matches, opponents’ stepping movements were coupled in two distinct modes: at close range they moved in anti-phase, maintaining a safe distance, while from farther away they switched abruptly to in-phase movement to close the gap. The switch happened at a critical interpersonal distance, a sudden transition between two stable coordination patterns (Okumura et al., 2012).

● Evidence: well-established

Coordination patterns self-organize and switch. Human movement coordination shows stable patterns and abrupt transitions between them as conditions change, as described by the HKB model and confirmed across many tasks (Haken et al., 1985; Kelso & Schöner, 1988). Similar transitions appear between opponents in kendo (Okumura et al., 2012).

What does this have to do with a micro-vortex? Perhaps a good deal, in principle. The system describes each transition, from punch to elbow, from elbow to backward hammerfist, from hammerfist to lateral elbow, as a “momentum switch.” In the language of coordination dynamics, each strike might be a temporarily stable pattern, and each switch a transition triggered when the motion, the rebound, and the arm’s position reach a certain state. If so, the sequence would “feel automatic” for a good reason: the body is not choosing each strike, it is falling from one stable pattern into the next.

That is a hypothesis, not a finding. Nobody has measured the micro-vortex. But it is a much better hypothesis than “fractal kinetic chaining,” because it can be tested: a motion-capture study would show whether the transitions occur at consistent joint angles or speeds, and whether they become more consistent with practice.

Why the pattern feels automatic

The project materials say the micro-vortex feels automatic once the wave is initiated. That, too, has a scientific counterpart.

When people practise a sequence of movements, the brain gradually groups the elements into chunks: short runs of movements executed as a unit, with pauses between chunks rather than between each element. In a classic study of visuomotor sequence learning, people spontaneously organized long sequences into chunks, and the chunks became their own units of performance (Sakai et al., 2003). Brain imaging has since shown that different brain networks are associated with binding elements together into chunks and with parsing sequences into separate chunks, and that chunks grow stronger over days of training (Wymbs et al., 2012).

A five-element loop, practised thousands of times, is exactly the kind of thing that becomes a chunk. Once it does, starting it may be enough to run it through, which is what “automatic” feels like from the inside.

There is a cost to automaticity, too. A chunk that runs on its own is hard to interrupt. That is useful if the situation is predictable. It is less useful against a live opponent who moves, or when the person in front of you turns out not to be a threat at all. Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 return to this.

● Evidence: well-established

Practised sequences become chunks. With practice, the brain groups movement sequences into chunks that are executed as units (Sakai et al., 2003; Wymbs et al., 2012). This is a general finding about sequence learning; it has not been studied in the micro-vortex specifically.

“Four to five impacts in under a second”

The project materials describe the micro-vortex as producing “4–5 stacked impacts in under one second” on or near the same target. Is that plausible?

As a matter of timing, yes. The path is described as small, about 8 to 14 inches (roughly 20 to 35 centimetres) per circle. Boxers’ hands have been measured moving at average speeds of about 6 to 8 metres per second at contact, with peaks above 12 metres per second (Whiting et al., 1988). Even at a much lower average speed of, say, 3 metres per second, a 30-centimetre segment of path would take about a tenth of a second. Five such segments, with brief contacts, could fit within a second. That is simple arithmetic, not a measurement, and it says nothing about how forceful each impact would be.

As a matter of effect, the claim is untested and much harder. Several questions are open:

  • Does each impact carry meaningful force, or are the later ones light taps riding on the rebound?
  • Does the “same spot” really get hit again, or does the target (or a person) move after the first impact?
  • Do the impacts “stack” in any meaningful sense? Repeated impacts on a heavy bag add up only as separate events; there is no evidence of “compounding resonance.”
  • Does the sequence survive contact with a target that does not behave like a freestanding bag?

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Stacked impacts and compounding resonance are untested. The claim of 4–5 impacts in under a second is plausible as a cadence but has not been filmed or measured. “Compounding resonance” has no support in physics or biomechanics. Chapter 13 describes a simple filmed test that would settle the cadence question and give a first look at the force question.

Geometry as a teaching image

If the physics of “toroidal fields” is not real, is the geometry useless? Not at all.

Images like figure-eights, spirals, and loops can be powerful teaching cues. They give a learner a single, simple picture that organizes many joints at once. Research on attentional focus, discussed in Book 1, has found that directing attention to the effect of a movement, rather than to the body parts producing it, generally improves both performance and learning (Wulf, 2013). “Trace a figure-eight with the fist” or “let the elbow follow the circle” are effect-focused cues of exactly this kind. They may help because they are not anatomical instructions.

The figure-eight also has a long history as a symbol, and it would be strange to ask practitioners not to find meaning in it. An anthropologist of martial arts has even used the “infinity loop” as a model for how efficacy and performance feed each other in martial traditions, while warning that when the two collide, practitioners can be misled into false beliefs about what works (Farrer, 2015). That double lesson is worth keeping: the loop can inspire, and it can deceive.

Inevitability, revisited

The system’s name rests on a psychological claim: that its motion feels “predestined” to the opponent because it emerges from universal patterns. The materials call this “psychological inevitability.”

What would that mean, scientifically? Expert fighters are very good at anticipating what an opponent will do from early cues in their movement (Mori et al., 2002; Mann et al., 2007), and they pick up repeated patterns quickly (Milazzo et al., 2016). A fighter whose sequences are unpredictable might make that anticipation harder. On the other hand, a fighter who always runs the same loop would become more predictable, not less, to an experienced opponent. The claim cuts both ways, and only testing against skilled, resisting partners could tell which way it cuts for this system. Chapter 9 looks at this research in more detail.

A pattern that emerges is beautiful. A pattern that repeats is readable.

Breath

Chapter 7

Inhale on compression, exhale on release. — breath synchronization, from the project materials

Every martial tradition seems to have something to say about breathing. Karate has the kiai, the sharp shout at the moment of a strike. Boxers hiss or grunt as they punch. Tai chi teaches slow, deep breathing coordinated with movement. Russian Systema, which the System of Inevitability names as a parallel path, places breath and relaxation at its very centre. The System of Inevitability itself recommends synchronizing the breath with the wave: inhale on compression, exhale on release.

Breathing does at least three different jobs in a striking art. It braces the trunk. It may amplify force at the moment of effort. And it regulates the nervous system, the state of calm or arousal in which every decision is made. The science of each job is different, and it is worth taking them one at a time.

Breath as brace

When you lift something heavy, you probably hold your breath without thinking. That is not an accident. Holding a breath after inhaling raises the pressure inside the abdomen, which stiffens the trunk. In a study that measured intra-abdominal pressure during lifting, holding the breath after an inhalation produced significantly greater peak pressure than natural breathing, holding after an exhalation, or breathing out during the lift (Hagins et al., 2004).

Stiffening the trunk is useful in striking, too. The first peak of McGill’s “double peak” (Chapter 5) seems to be about creating a stable core for the limbs to work against (McGill et al., 2010). But breath-holding has a cost that matters for anyone training hard. During heavy straining with the breath held, a manoeuvre called the Valsalva manoeuvre, blood pressure can rise to extreme levels. In experienced bodybuilders, directly measured arterial pressures during heavy leg presses averaged 320/250 mmHg, and exceeded 480/350 in one person (MacDougall et al., 1985).

⚠ Caution

Don’t hold your breath through repeated strikes. Long breath-holds under maximal effort cause extreme spikes in blood pressure (MacDougall et al., 1985). If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, eye conditions such as glaucoma or retinal problems, or a history of stroke or aneurysm, speak to a physician before any hard striking or straining. In the micro-vortex and bag work, keep breathing: short, sharp exhalations with strikes are generally safer than holding.

Breath as amplifier

What about shouting or grunting? It sounds like folklore, but it has been tested.

In a study of 50 martial artists, 25 novices and 25 experts, handgrip strength was significantly greater when participants shouted a kiap (the Korean equivalent of the kiai) than when they did not: about 437 newtons compared with 408 (Welch & Tschampl, 2012). In collegiate tennis players, serve and forehand velocities and isometric force were significantly greater when players grunted, and peak muscle activity in the chest and trunk muscles was higher too (O’Connell et al., 2014).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

A sharp exhalation or shout may boost force slightly. Shouting during effort increased grip strength in martial artists, and grunting increased stroke velocity and force in tennis players (Welch & Tschampl, 2012; O’Connell et al., 2014). The effects are modest and come from a small number of studies; how they work (trunk stiffening, arousal, or attention) is not settled.

The system’s instruction, exhale on release, is consistent with these findings. A forceful exhalation at the moment of the strike may help coordinate the trunk’s stiffening with the impact, the second peak of the double peak. Whether a specific breath pattern improves the micro-vortex has not been tested.

Breath as regulator

The third job of breathing is the one that matters most for the “consciousness” theme of this series, and for the ethics chapters to come.

Breathing is unique among the body’s automatic functions: it runs by itself, but you can take it over at will. And the way you breathe changes the state of your nervous system. A systematic review of slow-breathing studies found that breathing at slow rates, below ten breaths a minute, was associated with increased heart-rate variability and markers of parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) activity, and with increased comfort, relaxation, vigour, and alertness, along with reduced arousal, anxiety, anger, and confusion (Zaccaro et al., 2018). The mechanism is partly understood: slow breathing interacts with the heart’s natural rhythm and with the reflexes that regulate blood pressure, which is the basis of heart-rate-variability biofeedback (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).

A randomized controlled study compared three daily five-minute breathing practices with mindfulness meditation over a month. Breathing with extended exhalations, called cyclic sighing, produced greater improvement in mood and a greater reduction in breathing rate than mindfulness meditation did (Balban et al., 2023).

● Evidence: well-established

Slow breathing calms the nervous system. Slow, controlled breathing is reliably associated with increased heart-rate variability and reduced arousal and anxiety (Zaccaro et al., 2018; Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). Brief daily breathing practices with long exhalations improved mood in a randomized study (Balban et al., 2023). Effects on performance in combat have not been directly tested.

This is where breath stops being a technique for hitting harder and becomes a technique for choosing well. Chapter 10 looks at what stress does to perception and decisions, and how breathing and attention training can help. Chapter 11 argues that the most important strike a practitioner can learn to “time” is the one they don’t throw.

Systema: what is and isn’t known

The project materials present Russian Systema as a “parallel path up the same mountain,” sharing with the System of Inevitability an emphasis on continuous flow, natural movement, relaxation, breath, and wave-like motion. They also describe Systema as “used by Spetsnaz/FSB.”

Here this book has to be careful.

First, as of the time of writing, this book could not find any peer-reviewed study of Systema: no biomechanical analysis, no training study, no outcome data. Searches of the scholarly indexes used to verify every reference in this book returned nothing on Systema specifically. That does not mean Systema is ineffective. It means its claims, like the System of Inevitability’s, have not been tested in published research.

Second, the association between Systema and Russian special forces is widely repeated in popular and commercial sources, but this book could not verify it in any scholarly source. It is best treated as part of the art’s own story about itself, not as evidence of effectiveness. Even if a military unit uses a method, that tells us it was chosen, not that it was tested against alternatives.

Third, the principles the two systems share, relaxation, breath control, and continuous adaptive movement, do have research behind them, and much of it is in this book: the double peak of relaxation and stiffening (Chapter 5), breath and arousal (this chapter), variable practice (Chapter 8), and calm under pressure (Chapter 10). The parallel between the two systems is real at the level of principle. It is unverified at the level of outcomes.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Systema parallels are conceptual. The shared emphasis on breath, relaxation, and flow is a reasonable philosophical parallel. No peer-reviewed research on Systema was found; claims about its military use could not be verified in scholarly sources and should not be treated as validation of either system.

A simple breathing practice

Here is a practice that draws on the research above and costs nothing. It is a suggestion, not part of the System of Inevitability.

  1. Before training, sit or stand quietly for two minutes. Breathe in through the nose, take a second small “top-up” inhalation, then breathe out slowly through the mouth, longer than the inhalation. This is the cyclic sigh studied by Balban et al. (2023). Notice your shoulders and hands soften.
  2. During slow wave practice, let the breath follow the movement as the system suggests: in as the body gathers and compresses, out as it releases. Keep it unhurried.
  3. During bag work, use short, sharp exhalations with strikes. Never hold your breath through a sequence.
  4. After training, return to the slow breathing for a minute, and notice how quickly your heart rate settles. Over weeks, that recovery is a small measure of your nervous system’s growing flexibility.

The breath is the one door between the part of you that reacts and the part of you that chooses.

Part III · The Learning

Repetition without repetition. The same problem, solved a little differently every time.

Never the Same Strike Twice

Chapter 8

The practitioner does not pre-plan sequences; geometry and bag feedback generate patterns on the fly. — from the System of Inevitability project materials

Most traditional martial arts are taught by repetition. A student practises a punch, a block, or a form hundreds of times, in exactly the same way, until it is “grooved.” The System of Inevitability takes a different view. It describes itself as non-repetitive: combinations are not memorized but generated afresh, “fractal” chains emerging from a few principles and from the feedback of the bag or dummy. In Book 1 we saw the same idea in its juggling: patterns that are never quite the same twice.

Is that a good way to learn? This is one of the places where the system’s philosophy meets a large and lively body of research, with real support and real controversy.

Variability is not the enemy

For much of the twentieth century, variability in movement was treated as noise: error to be stamped out by repetition. The Russian physiologist Nikolai Bernstein famously described skilled practice instead as “repetition without repetition,” solving the same motor problem again and again, each time slightly differently. Modern research has given that idea substance.

In a pair of experiments on how people learn new arm movements, people who naturally showed more task-relevant variability in their movements learned faster, both across individuals and across tasks. The researchers also found that training could reshape the structure of a person’s variability to suit the task. Variability, in other words, is partly how the nervous system explores (Wu et al., 2014).

A long line of research on contextual interference, discussed in Book 1, points the same way. When people practise several skills in a mixed, random order rather than in blocks of the same skill, they usually perform worse during practice but remember and transfer the skills better later (Shea & Morgan, 1979). Later experiments helped separate two ingredients: the benefit of mixing different kinds of movements, and the benefit of varying the parameters of one kind of movement (Hall & Magill, 1995).

● Evidence: well-established

Variable practice generally helps learning. Task-relevant motor variability predicts faster learning (Wu et al., 2014). Mixed or random practice usually impairs performance during training but improves retention and transfer compared with blocked repetition (Shea & Morgan, 1979; Hall & Magill, 1995).

Differential learning: promise and controversy

One approach takes variability to an extreme. Differential learning, developed by the German sport scientist Wolfgang Schöllhorn, deliberately adds large, ever-changing variations to practice: no two attempts are the same, and learners are not corrected toward a single ideal form. The theory is that the nervous system finds its own solution by sampling widely around it.

Some studies have found impressive effects. In one, semi-professional badminton players showed different patterns of brain activity after differential training than after repetitive training, which the authors interpreted as faster early consolidation of learning (Henz & Schöllhorn, 2016).

But the overall evidence is more cautious. An exploratory meta-analysis gathered 27 studies comparing differential learning with other methods. It found a small advantage during acquisition and a medium advantage at retention, but warned that the studies were heterogeneous, small, at high risk of bias, and possibly affected by publication bias, so that “inferences about the effectiveness of DL would be premature” (Tassignon et al., 2021). Schöllhorn and colleagues have responded by arguing that the debate depends heavily on which model of motor learning a researcher assumes, and that individual learners in dynamic situations may not follow any one general rule (Schöllhorn et al., 2022).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Highly variable “differential” practice is promising but unproven. Some studies find advantages for differential learning, and a meta-analysis found small-to-medium average benefits, but with high risk of bias and large heterogeneity (Tassignon et al., 2021). The method’s developers and critics still disagree about how to interpret the evidence (Schöllhorn et al., 2022).

Constraints, not commands

A related family of ideas comes from ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach. In this view, a skill is not a stored program but a solution that emerges from the interaction of three kinds of constraints: the performer (body, fitness, intentions), the task (rules, goals, equipment), and the environment (surfaces, space, opponents). A coach shapes learning less by telling the learner what to do than by designing the problem: changing the constraints so that good solutions emerge (Renshaw et al., 2010). Applied to teaching, this is called nonlinear pedagogy: manipulating key constraints so that functional movement patterns and decisions emerge in learners (Chow et al., 2007). Decision-making in sport, on this view, emerges from the continuous coupling of the athlete and the environment rather than from a central plan (Araújo et al., 2006).

The System of Inevitability’s training on a freestanding bag and a metal-armed dummy is, in this language, a constraints-led practice. The bag’s rebound, its swing, and its weight shape the movements that emerge; the dummy’s rigid arms shape the alignment of the forearm and wrist. The practitioner does not decide in advance what to throw. The tools pose the problem.
