That is a real strength. But the constraints-led approach also insists on something the system’s solo tools cannot provide: representative design. Practice environments should faithfully represent the information and demands of the situation the skill is meant for (Pinder et al., 2011). A bag and a dummy represent some of the demands of close-range fighting, such as contact, rebound, and alignment. They do not represent the most important demand: another person who perceives, decides, and moves.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Designing the problem is a powerful way to teach. Constraints-led and nonlinear pedagogy approaches have a strong theoretical basis and growing empirical support (Renshaw et al., 2010; Chow et al., 2007; Araújo et al., 2006). Their own central principle, representative design, implies that solo tools must eventually be supplemented by practice with live partners (Pinder et al., 2011).

Silat’s answer: jazz

Here the anthropology of Silat offers a beautiful parallel. In a study of Sundanese pencak silat in West Java, the anthropologist Lee Wilson compared learning to improvise in silat with learning to improvise jazz piano. In both, he argued, improvisation is not random: it is a highly structured process that proceeds from mastering a few generic principles, from which “potentially unbounded repertoires” of responses can be generated. He contrasted this with the nationally standardized form of silat, in which the generative potential of the practice was subordinated to the goal of uniformity (Wilson, 2009).

The System of Inevitability’s claim to be non-repetitive and principle-based is, in this light, part of an old and respected tradition, one that a scholarly study has described from inside the Silat lineage the system cites. It also suggests what “non-repetitive” should mean in practice: not anything goes, but a small set of well-learned principles applied freshly each time.

Implicit learning and the trouble with thinking

One more strand of research supports the system’s preference for emergent over explained movement. When people learn a skill with a great deal of conscious, explicit knowledge of the rules, they can be more likely to break down under pressure, because pressure tempts them to consciously monitor and control the movement. Learners who acquire the same skill more implicitly, with less rule-knowledge, may be more robust (Masters, 1992). Studies of “choking” have found that pressure can harm skilled performance by drawing attention to processes that run best without it (Beilock & Carr, 2001). And as Book 1 discussed, directing attention to the effect of movement rather than to the body generally helps learning (Wulf, 2013).

A practice built on images (waves, loops, figure-eights) and on feedback from a tool, rather than on detailed joint-by-joint instruction, may favour exactly this kind of robust, implicit learning. That is a reasonable hypothesis. It has not been tested in this system.

Where non-repetition can go wrong

Variability is not a magic ingredient. Three cautions follow from the research:

  1. Variability around what? Wu and colleagues found that task-relevant variability helped. Random flailing is not task-relevant. The system’s principles (alignment, the wave, the lock at impact) are what make its variability meaningful. Without them, variation is just noise.
  2. Safety needs consistency. Some things should never vary: the wrist must be aligned and braced at impact, every time. A practice that varies the path of a strike can still be strict about structure at contact.
  3. Solo variability is not opponent variability. A bag varies in predictable physical ways. A person varies intelligently, and tries to make you miss. The next chapter turns to what research says about learning to deal with that.

Freedom in the path. Discipline at the point of contact.

Reading the Other

Chapter 9

A bag swings back. A person decides.

Everything in the last few chapters, the wave, the double peak, the micro-vortex, can be practised alone. That is one of the System of Inevitability’s great strengths: like Book 1’s iron balls and ring bar, its striking tools need no partner, no gym, and no instructor. It is also its greatest limitation as a martial system, and the materials themselves acknowledge it when they say that full viability requires “progressive pressure-testing.” This chapter explains, from the research, why.

Combat is a conversation

A group of researchers in the Netherlands and Britain have argued that combat sports should be understood as an interpersonal synergy. In a fight, two athletes continuously co-adapt to each other: each perceives the other’s possibilities for attack and defence, and each acts on those perceptions, so that the two of them self-organize into a single coupled system. Skilled fighters, they argue, operate in “meta-stable regions on the limits of their capabilities,” exploiting moments when the coupling becomes unstable. They reviewed evidence that expert fighters perceive their own and their opponents’ action boundaries accurately, and that local actions of each fighter produce synchronization at the level of the whole fight (Krabben et al., 2019). The kendo study of the last chapter, with its sudden switch between coordination modes at a critical distance, is one example (Okumura et al., 2012).

If that view is right, then the most important skills in close-range combat are not the strikes themselves but the perception and timing that decide when, where, and whether to strike.

What experts see

There is strong evidence that expertise in combat sports is, to a large degree, perceptual.

In a study of karate athletes and novices, the athletes were faster at a choice-reaction task when the stimulus was video of an opponent’s attack, deciding whether it was aimed high or middle, but not when the stimulus was simple dots. Their simple reaction times were no faster than novices’. And when the video was cut off very early in the attack, the athletes were still much more accurate at predicting where it was going (Mori et al., 2002). Experts, in other words, are not faster in general. They are better at reading the specific information that matters.

A meta-analysis across many sports found that experts consistently outperform non-experts in perceptual-cognitive skills: they pick up cues earlier, anticipate more accurately, and use their eyes more efficiently (Mann et al., 2007). In on-mat karate tasks, experts were faster and more accurate at blocking and counter-attacking, detected a repeated attack pattern after only five repetitions while novices did not, and used a more efficient visual search strategy, with fewer, longer fixations (Milazzo et al., 2016).

● Evidence: well-established

Expertise in fighting is perceptual. Expert combat athletes anticipate opponents’ actions from early cues and pick up patterns quickly, without being faster in simple reaction time (Mori et al., 2002; Mann et al., 2007; Milazzo et al., 2016).

These findings cut against the idea of a fixed, repeated sequence. Milazzo’s karate experts spotted a repeated attack after five repetitions. A fighter who always ran the same micro-vortex would be handing a skilled opponent the same gift. The system’s emphasis on “non-repetitive” chaining is, in this light, exactly right in principle. But it can only be learned against someone who is trying to read you.

The bag does not read you

A freestanding heavy bag and a metal-armed dummy provide real physical feedback: contact, rebound, resistance, alignment. They do not provide the information a fighter must learn to read, and they never try to read the fighter in return.

Research on training specificity shows how much this matters. In a study of mixed martial arts athletes wearing accelerometers, the same techniques (jabs, crosses, hooks) produced significantly different loads when performed in isolation than when performed in sparring, and the patterns of difference between techniques also changed (Kirk et al., 2015). A strike practised alone is, physically and perceptually, not quite the same movement as a strike thrown at a person who is moving.

And as Book 1 discussed, skills learned in one context generally transfer poorly to distant ones. Training in chess, music, or working-memory tasks does not reliably improve unrelated abilities (Sala & Gobet, 2017). Close transfer, from one setting to a similar one, is far more reliable than far transfer. A bag is a moderately close relative of a person. It is not a twin.

● Evidence: well-established

Practice is specific. The same techniques produce different movement loads alone and in sparring (Kirk et al., 2015), and far transfer between dissimilar tasks is weak (Sala & Gobet, 2017). Representative practice, which preserves the information of the real situation, is needed for skills to transfer (Pinder et al., 2011).

What winners do

Studies of real bouts give a picture of what actually decides close-range fights in sport. In an analysis of 33 elite amateur boxing bouts, winners threw more punches, more combinations, and used defensive skills more effectively, with defence integrated with movement of the arms, feet, and trunk (Ashker, 2011). The physiological demands of amateur boxing are substantial and predominantly aerobic: a three-round bout against pads modelled on competition required a large aerobic energy contribution (Davis et al., 2014), and reviews describe amateur boxing as a high-intensity, intermittent sport that demands high cardiorespiratory fitness, anaerobic power, strength, and muscular power in both the upper and lower limbs (Chaabène et al., 2015; Slimani et al., 2017).

These are findings from a sport with rules, gloves, and a referee, and they do not translate directly to the system’s close-quarters setting. But they underline something the system’s materials sometimes overlook: in any real exchange, defence, footwork, perception, and conditioning decide as much as the elegance of an attacking sequence.

“Psychological inevitability” and the opponent’s mind

The system’s name rests on a claim about the opponent: that its motions feel “predestined” because they arise from universal patterns, so that the opponent “fights the geometry rather than a person.”

Is there anything in the research that could support or refute this? Indirectly, yes. Expert fighters thrive on predictable information (Milazzo et al., 2016); unpredictability is what makes their anticipation fail. A system that genuinely generates fresh, non-repeating combinations from principles could make an opponent’s anticipation harder. That would be a meaningful advantage. But no study has tested whether this system does that, and the experience of feeling “inevitable” from the inside is not evidence of what an opponent experiences.

The only way to find out is to ask opponents, under controlled conditions, with something at stake. Chapter 13 suggests how.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“Psychological inevitability” is untested. Whether opponents experience the system’s motion as unreadable or “predestined” has never been studied. Research on anticipation suggests that genuinely unpredictable sequences could be an advantage, while repeated ones would quickly become readable to a skilled opponent.

Partners, not targets

If perception and timing can only be learned against a person, then the most important training tool is not the bag or the dummy. It is a partner: someone who will move, feint, resist, and give honest feedback, at an intensity both of you can control.

That changes the nature of practice. A bag cannot be hurt. A partner can. From this point on, the science of skill and the ethics of training are inseparable. Chapter 11 sets out what that means, and Chapter 13 describes a graduated way of testing with partners that keeps both people safe. First, though, we need to look at what happens to all of these skills when fear enters the room.

The bag teaches the hand. Only a person can teach the eyes.

Calm Under Pressure

Chapter 10

Fear narrows the world. Training can widen it again.

Every skill in this book was described as if it would be performed calmly: a relaxed swing, a well-timed stiffening, an open, perceptive attention to the other person. Real confrontations are not calm. The heart pounds, the breath shortens, vision narrows, hands shake, and thinking becomes simple and urgent. For a martial art, and for any person who hopes to behave well when it matters, what happens to skill and judgement under that kind of pressure is perhaps the most important question of all.

Fortunately it is one of the best-studied.

What fear does to skill

According to attentional control theory, anxiety impairs the brain’s goal-directed attention system and strengthens the stimulus-driven one: attention is pulled toward threats and away from the task. Anxious people may still perform well if they compensate with extra effort, but their processing becomes less efficient (Eysenck et al., 2007). A review focused on perceptual-motor performance proposed an integrated model in which anxiety can affect what people perceive, how they interpret it, and how they act, sometimes for better but often for worse (Nieuwenhuys & Oudejans, 2012).

The most vivid evidence comes from police officers, who have to perform physical skills under real threat. In one study, officers’ arrest and self-defence skills, rated on a carefully validated five-point scale, deteriorated markedly when they were performed under pressure (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009). In another, officers kicked, blocked, or restrained an opponent attacking with either a rubber knife or a knife that delivered a real electric shock. Under the higher threat, performance was worse, and full-body movement analysis revealed avoidance: faster but poorer reactions, leaning backward when kicking, ducking when blocking (Renden et al., 2014). The officers’ bodies were trying to get away from the threat even while they were trying to deal with it.

● Evidence: well-established

Pressure degrades skill. Anxiety shifts attention toward threat and away from the task, reducing processing efficiency (Eysenck et al., 2007). Police officers’ arrest and self-defence skills deteriorate under pressure, and movement takes on features of avoidance (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009; Renden et al., 2014).

This matters for the micro-vortex and every other sequence in this book. A pattern practised only in calm conditions, against a bag that never threatens, has not been tested in the conditions where it would matter most.

Training with fear

The encouraging part of this research is that the effects of pressure can be trained.

In one study, police officers practised handgun shooting either against cardboard targets or against a live opponent firing back with coloured soap cartridges. At the start, both groups shot worse when the opponent fired back. After just three one-hour training sessions, the group that had trained under pressure no longer got worse under pressure, while the other group still did (Oudejans, 2008). A follow-up found the benefit was still present four months later (Nieuwenhuys & Oudejans, 2011). Expert basketball players and darts players showed the same pattern: only those who practised with anxiety maintained their performance in an anxious test (Oudejans & Pijpers, 2009).

A meta-analysis of stress inoculation training, which deliberately prepares people for stress through information, skills practice, and graduated exposure, pooled 37 studies with 1,837 participants. It found that the approach reduced performance anxiety and state anxiety and improved performance under stress, across a range of settings and trainer experience (Saunders et al., 1996).

Martial arts experience may help too, although it does not make anyone immune. Police officers who did additional martial arts training, even once a week, performed arrest and self-defence skills better under high anxiety than officers without such training; but they still performed worse under high anxiety than under low (Renden et al., 2015).

● Evidence: well-established

Pressure can be trained. Practising under realistic, graduated pressure protects performance under pressure, in police officers and athletes, with effects lasting months (Oudejans, 2008; Nieuwenhuys & Oudejans, 2011; Oudejans & Pijpers, 2009). Stress inoculation training reduces anxiety and improves performance under stress (Saunders et al., 1996).

Mindfulness under fire

Book 1 discussed the evidence on mindfulness meditation, which is real but more modest than its popular image (Goyal et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2015; Van Dam et al., 2018). Two studies of military personnel speak directly to pressure.

In a study of soldiers in the high-stress period before deployment, working-memory capacity declined over time in soldiers who did not receive mindfulness training. Among those who did, working memory increased in those who practised a lot, and declined in those who practised little. More practice was also associated with less negative and more positive mood (Jha et al., 2010). In a larger controlled study, eight platoons of Marines (281 people) took part: four received an eight-week mindfulness-based training emphasizing interoceptive awareness and attentional control, and four continued training as usual. After a stressful combat-training exercise, the mindfulness group showed faster recovery of heart rate and breathing rate, along with differences in brain activity in regions involved in interoception, including the insula (Johnson et al., 2014).

Interoception, the sense of what is happening inside the body, connects these findings to the system’s emphasis on breath and relaxation. Book 1 introduced the insula’s role in bodily awareness (Craig, 2009). A review of contemplative practice and health has argued that how people interpret their bodily sensations lies at the heart of many stress-related problems, and that contemplative practices may reduce maladaptive interpretations and restore a sense of presence and agency (Farb et al., 2015). In combat terms: the pounding heart is not the problem. The story you tell yourself about the pounding heart may be.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Mindfulness may protect attention and speed recovery under stress. Mindfulness training was associated with protected working memory in soldiers who practised more (Jha et al., 2010) and faster physiological recovery after stressful training in Marines (Johnson et al., 2014). These are promising controlled studies, not the final word; effects depended on practice time.

Calm as a decision skill

The most direct test of calm as a decision skill comes from policing. In a randomized pilot study, police officers were trained in techniques to enhance psychological and physiological control during stressful incidents, and then tested in realistic critical-incident scenarios. The trained group showed significantly better physiological control, better situational awareness, better overall performance, and more correct use-of-force decisions than the control group (Andersen & Gustafsberg, 2016).

This is a small pilot study, and it needs replication. But it points toward the deepest connection between this chapter and the next: physiological calm is not only about performing a technique well. It is about seeing clearly enough to choose the right action, which is very often no strike at all.

Calm is not the absence of fear. It is the presence of choice.

Building pressure into practice

How could a practitioner of the System of Inevitability build these findings into solo training, before ever stepping in front of a partner? Some suggestions, which are my and not the system’s:

  • Breath before, during, and after. Use the slow, long-exhale breathing from Chapter 7 to begin and end every session, and notice how quickly you return to calm after hard bag work. Recovery is trainable (Johnson et al., 2014).
  • Mild, graded pressure. Add small stressors that do not increase injury risk: a timer, a partner calling out random cues, being filmed, an audience of one. The research on training with anxiety suggests that even mild pressure helps performance transfer to pressured conditions (Oudejans & Pijpers, 2009).
  • Never raise physical risk to create pressure. Hitting harder, faster, or on a harder target when you’re stressed is how hands break. Raise the psychological stakes, not the physical ones.
  • Practise the decision, not only the strike. Have a partner present cues that call for different responses, including not striking, stepping away, or speaking. A decision that is never practised will not appear under pressure.

These are the bridges from solo practice to the partner work and testing described in Chapter 13. But before any of that, there is a question this book must ask clearly: what is all this skill for?

Part IV · The Responsibility

The hand that can strike must learn, first and last, when not to.

The Ethics of the Closed Hand

Chapter 11

The upgrade is not the power to harm. It is becoming trustworthy with it.

This is the most important chapter in the book.

Everything so far has been about capability: how a fist holds together, how a wave travels through a body, how a sequence becomes automatic, how skill survives under pressure. A person who develops those capabilities has become, in a precise and literal sense, more dangerous. The System of Inevitability describes itself as an engine “for close-quarters dominance.” This series of books exists to help facilitate what its owner calls an upgrade in human consciousness. Those two things can only be reconciled in one way: if the growth in capability is matched, and exceeded, by growth in self-mastery, restraint, judgement, and care.

This chapter is about that second growth. It draws on research where research exists, and it is honest about where ethics has to go beyond what can be measured.

What a strike can do

Start with the plain facts, because they are sobering.

A single punch can kill. In Australia, a study of coronial records identified 90 deaths between 2000 and 2012 from “king hits,” single blows to the head that caused the victim to fall unconscious, either from the punch itself or from the head striking the ground. Most occurred at or near hotels and pubs, late at night, and alcohol was involved in about three quarters of the cases where toxicology was available (Pilgrim et al., 2014). Many of those who threw the punches presumably did not intend to kill anyone.

In a study designed to estimate head-injury risk, straight punches from Olympic boxers to an instrumented crash-test dummy head produced peak head accelerations averaging about 58 g (Walilko et al., 2005). Trained self-defence practitioners striking from a dominant ground position could, with elbow and palm strikes, exceed a force associated with skull fracture in a substantial fraction of strikes (Beranek et al., 2020). Repeated blows to the head over time are linked to lasting brain injury; the condition now called chronic traumatic encephalopathy was first described in boxers in 1928 (Bernick & Banks, 2013). In mixed martial arts, the head is the most commonly injured region, and concussion is common (Lystad et al., 2014; Curran-Sills & Abedin, 2018).

The System of Inevitability emphasizes elbows, hammerfists, forearms, and repeated strikes to the same spot, at the closest range, against the head and neck as readily as anywhere else. Whatever its effectiveness, its potential for serious harm is not in doubt.

● Evidence: well-established

Strikes can cause catastrophic harm. Single blows to the head can kill, often through the fall that follows (Pilgrim et al., 2014). Elbow and palm strikes can reach forces associated with skull fracture (Beranek et al., 2020). Repeated head impacts are associated with long-term brain injury (Bernick & Banks, 2013).

What violence is

Scholars of martial arts have long wrestled with what they call a violence paradox: how can a practice built around destructive, antisocial techniques become, in the training hall, a source of positive, productive, even edifying experience? In a recent theoretical paper, two scholars proposed that violence is best understood not as a type of movement but as a characteristic of an interaction, defined as “violation by intentional force” (Channon & Matthews, 2026).

That definition is useful for a practitioner. The same elbow can be a skilled movement on a bag, a controlled exchange with a consenting partner, a necessary act of protection, or a violation. What makes the difference is not the geometry. It is consent, necessity, proportion, and intention. A martial art does not make its practitioners violent or non-violent. What they choose does.

Does martial arts training make people better?

It is often said that martial arts teach discipline, respect, and self-control. Is it true? The honest answer is: sometimes, and it depends.

On the encouraging side, a meta-analysis of 14 studies found that martial arts training had a small positive effect on wellbeing and a medium effect on reducing internalizing problems such as anxiety and depression, although its effect on aggression was close to zero and not significant (Moore et al., 2020). A separate meta-analysis of 12 child and youth studies (507 participants) found that in the nine intervention and longitudinal studies, martial arts training reduced aggression and related externalizing behaviour with a medium effect size (Harwood et al., 2017). In a study in which 207 schoolchildren were randomly assigned by class to three months of school-based Tae Kwon Do or ordinary physical education, the martial arts group improved more in cognitive and emotional self-regulation, prosocial behaviour, and classroom conduct (Lakes & Hoyt, 2004).

On the cautionary side, a multilevel meta-analysis of 12 studies with nearly 6,000 young people found no overall relationship between martial arts participation and externalizing behaviour. It found signs of publication bias in favour of positive results; after adjusting for it, martial arts participation was associated with more externalizing behaviour. Studies with more intense training also found more externalizing behaviour (Gubbels et al., 2016). A two-year longitudinal study of 477 Norwegian boys found that taking part in “power sports,” including boxing, wrestling, weightlifting, and oriental martial arts, led to increased violent and non-violent antisocial behaviour outside sport. The authors attributed this partly to the sports themselves and partly to repeated contact with “macho” attitudes and norms (Endresen & Olweus, 2005).

Two older studies hint at why the findings diverge. In a six-month study of juvenile delinquents, those taught traditional Tae Kwon Do, with its psychological and philosophical teachings, became less aggressive and less anxious, while those taught a “modern” version stripped of those teachings became more aggressive and more delinquent (Trulson, 1986). In a cross-sectional study of traditional karate students, longer training was associated with lower aggressiveness (Nosanchuk, 1981). These are small, old studies and should not carry too much weight. But they point the same way as the larger reviews: what is taught alongside the techniques matters.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Martial arts can improve wellbeing and self-control, but not automatically. Meta-analyses find benefits for wellbeing and internalizing problems (Moore et al., 2020) and, in intervention studies with youth, reduced aggression (Harwood et al., 2017). Other meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence finds no benefit or even harm, especially with intense training and “macho” cultures (Gubbels et al., 2016; Endresen & Olweus, 2005). Training that explicitly includes ethical and psychological teaching appears more beneficial (Trulson, 1986).

The solo practitioner’s burden

This research has a pointed implication for the System of Inevitability. “No instructors required. No belts.” That is a liberating idea for conditioning and skill. But in the studies above, the instructor and the training culture seem to be among the main channels through which martial arts’ good effects, or bad ones, are delivered. A solitary practitioner has no teacher to model restraint, no community to frown at bravado, and no tradition to remind them what the skill is for.

That means the practitioner has to supply those things themselves. This book suggests four:

  1. A purpose. Decide, in writing, why you train. “To protect myself and others when there is truly no other option, and to become calmer, stronger, and more aware” is a purpose. “To dominate” is not.
  2. A code. Adopt explicit rules for the use of force (below), and review them regularly.
  3. A witness. Train sometimes with others, and invite feedback not only on technique but on attitude.
  4. A practice of restraint. Train walking away, speaking calmly, and stepping back as deliberately as you train striking.

De-escalation is a skill, and it can be trained

The most important “technique” in self-protection is not a strike. It is the ability to keep a situation from becoming a fight. Here, too, there is research.

A systematic review of 64 evaluations of de-escalation training, mostly in nursing and psychiatry, found that such training generally led to slight-to-moderate improvements with few adverse effects, though the quality of most studies was weak (Engel et al., 2020). Then came a stronger test. In a stepped-wedge randomized trial with a large city police department, a de-escalation training programme was followed by a 28% reduction in use-of-force incidents, a 26% reduction in injuries to citizens, and a 36% reduction in injuries to officers (Engel et al., 2022).

In another study, police officers who received a self-defence training that trained complete violent situations, not just physical skills, improved in communication, situational awareness, assertiveness, proportionality, and control. They “learned to use their actions before physical contact for de-escalation” (Renden et al., 2017).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

De-escalation training can reduce force and injuries. A randomized stepped-wedge trial in a police department found large reductions in use of force and in injuries to both citizens and officers after de-escalation training (Engel et al., 2022). Earlier evidence was mostly of low quality (Engel et al., 2020). Scenario-based training that includes communication improved officers’ proportionality and de-escalation (Renden et al., 2017).

The same lesson comes from research on self-defence for women. In a large randomized trial at three Canadian universities, a programme teaching women to assess risk from acquaintances, overcome emotional barriers to acknowledging danger, and use verbal and physical self-defence cut the one-year risk of completed rape almost in half, from 9.8% to 5.2% (Senn et al., 2015). A study of a feminist self-defence class found that participants were less likely to experience sexual assault over the following year and more confident in their ability to resist (Hollander, 2014). In both, the physical skills were only one part of a package built on awareness, recognition, and assertiveness.

Rules for the use of force

This book is not legal advice, and laws differ greatly between countries and states. Learn the law where you live from a qualified source. But the following principles, which are my suggestions, reflect a broad ethical consensus and the spirit of most self-defence law:

  • Avoid. The best fight is the one you are not in. Leave early. Cross the street. Let insults go.
  • De-escalate. Speak calmly, keep your hands open and visible, create distance, offer a way out.
  • Only when necessary. Use physical force only when there is an immediate threat of harm to you or someone else and no safer option exists.
  • Only as much as necessary. Use the least force that will stop the threat, and stop when it stops. A strike to escape is not a licence for a “micro-vortex” of five more.
  • Never as punishment, revenge, display, or test. Testing your system on strangers is assault.
  • Afterwards, care. Get to safety, call for help, seek medical attention for anyone injured, and tell the truth.

⚠ Caution

A note on the micro-vortex. A sequence designed to deliver four or five impacts to the same spot in under a second, if it works as described, is a sequence that can easily exceed what is necessary to stop a threat. Its automaticity (Chapter 6) makes this worse: a chunk, once started, is hard to stop. If you practise it, practise stopping it at every stage, on a cue, as diligently as you practise running it.

The people who train with you

A training partner who lets you strike near their face, or who resists you so that you can learn, is extending you an extraordinary trust. Sociologists of combat sports have described how practitioners manage risk through reflexivity and collaboration: the shared work of keeping a dangerous activity safe enough to learn from (Channon, 2020).

Some non-negotiables, again my suggestions:

  • Agree intensity before every round, and keep to it. If you want more, ask.
  • Control beats power. In partner work, the measure of skill is placing a strike precisely at an agreed intensity, not hitting hard.
  • Protect heads. No hard strikes to the head or neck in training, ever. Use headgear and gloves when any head contact is involved, and treat any suspected concussion as a reason to stop for the day and seek medical advice.
  • Have a stop word and a tap, and honour them instantly.
  • Partners are not test dummies. The metal-armed dummy is for full-force work. People are not.

The upgrade

So what does an upgrade in consciousness look like, in a person who trains to strike?

It looks like someone who can feel anger rise and watch it, the way they watch their breath, without being carried away by it. Someone who reads a room accurately, because their training taught them to read people, and who uses that skill to see trouble coming and step aside. Someone whose calm under pressure makes them the person others look to in an emergency. Someone who is gentle with weaker people because they have nothing to prove. Someone whose training partners trust them completely. Someone who could strike, and doesn’t.

None of that requires metaphysics. Every element of it has been touched, at least, by the research in this book: on attention and interoception, on calm under stress, on de-escalation, on the training cultures that make martial artists better or worse. It is an upgrade worth wanting, and it is available to anyone willing to practise it as seriously as they practise the fist.

Could strike. Doesn’t. That is the whole of the art.

The Safe Path for the Hand

Chapter 12

Bone and tendon keep their own calendar. They will not be hurried.

This chapter offers a suggested, conservative progression for training the bent fist, the wave, and the micro-vortex. It is my suggestion, drawn from the general literature on tissue adaptation, injury, and motor learning. It is not a formal syllabus, it has not been tested as a programme, and it does not replace a qualified coach, physiotherapist, or physician. Book 1 contains a similar progression for the iron balls and ring bar, and the two can be combined, but never increase load in both at once.

⚠ Caution

See a professional first if you have ever broken a bone in your hand or wrist, have wrist or elbow pain, numbness or tingling in your fingers, arthritis, osteoporosis or low bone density, a bleeding disorder, high blood pressure, heart disease, or eye problems, or if you are pregnant or take blood thinners. Striking is a high-impact activity for the hand, and heavy straining raises blood pressure (Chapter 7).

Five principles

1. The hand adapts slowly. Bone responds to loading, but on a scale of months and years. Studies of racquet and throwing athletes show that their loaded arms develop larger and stronger bones than their non-loaded arms, and that bone shape and size, not just density, change (Bass et al., 2002; Warden et al., 2014). Both studies also show that bone is most responsive to loading during youth; adults should expect slower and smaller gains. Tendons and ligaments adapt more slowly still: tendon stiffness changes in training studies lasting at least eight weeks, and the core of an adult tendon renews itself very little (Bohm et al., 2015; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019). Your striking surfaces will become more robust if you load them gradually, over many months. They will break if you hurry.

2. Short bouts, separated by rest. In a classic study in rats, the same daily number of loading cycles built stronger bone when split into four short bouts separated by hours than when given all at once (Robling et al., 2002). Bone cells desensitize to repeated loading and need time to recover their sensitivity. Researchers have used findings like this to suggest that exercise for bone should use brief, dynamic loading sessions with rest between them (Turner & Robling, 2003). Translated loosely to the hand: several short, light contact sessions a week are likely better than one long, hard one.

3. Avoid load spikes. Rapid increases in training load are a common contributor to injury, while gradually built capacity is protective (Gabbett, 2016). Increase one variable at a time: force, or duration, or target hardness, or speed, and by small steps.

4. Protect the hand, and the wrist behind it. Hand protection reduces hand injury in martial arts and boxing (Diesselhorst et al., 2013; Drury et al., 2017). Wraps and gloves are not a weakness. They are what elite boxers wear, and even elite boxers injure their hands (Loosemore et al., 2015).

5. Structure before speed, speed before power. Learn to hold the wrist aligned and the fist buttressed at the moment of contact slowly and lightly, before adding speed. Add speed before adding force. The “lock at impact” of “rock in a sock” (Chapter 5) must be automatic before you hit anything hard.

● Evidence: well-established

Gradual loading builds tissue; spikes break it. Bone and tendon adapt to progressive loading over months (Warden et al., 2014; Bohm et al., 2015). In rats, loading divided into short bouts with rest built stronger bone than the same load given at once (Robling et al., 2002). Rapid load increases are associated with injury (Gabbett, 2016).

About “hand conditioning”

Some martial traditions practise hand conditioning by repeatedly striking hard objects until calluses form. An early medical report on serious karate hand-conditioners found no X-ray evidence of damage to the knuckle bones in a small number of practitioners, but described a “savage technique” in which a callus is built over deliberately damaged tissue, and concluded that serious hand-conditioning was unnecessary for competition and “not recommended” (Larose & Sik, 1969). That study is old and tiny. Modern evidence about bone suggests a better route: moderate, progressive, dynamic loading with rest, rather than damage and repair.

The System of Inevitability’s metal-armed dummy, with arms of Schedule 40 steel pipe, provides exactly the “hard, unyielding feedback” the project materials praise. That is also what makes it dangerous to the unprepared. Steel does not yield; your hand must. The metal-armed dummy is the last tool in this progression, not the first.

A suggested progression

Stage Hand & wrist Striking work Contact & target Ready to progress when…
0. Foundation (4+ weeks) Wrist circles and flexion/extension through comfortable range; light grip and forearm work; practise a tight, buttressed conventional fist Slow whole-body wave in the air: ground, hips, trunk, arm, with breath None Full, pain-free wrist range; fist closes tightly without discomfort; no morning stiffness
1. Shape & slow wave (4–8 weeks) Form the J fist gently, unloaded; hold 5–10 s, release; compare its grip with a neutral fist Single-arm micro-vortex in the air, very slow, each station held briefly to check structure None: air only Can run the sequence slowly for 2–3 minutes per arm with wrist and elbow positions consistent on video
2. Touch (6–12 weeks) Wraps; static press of fist, hammerfist, and forearm into a soft bag, building to moderate pressure Light-touch strikes on a soft bag: conventional fist and hammerfist first, J fist last Soft or water bag; wraps and bag gloves No pain during or next morning; alignment holds on video at about half speed
3. Building force (3–6 months) Continue grip and forearm strength; monitor knuckles and wrist weekly Bag work at gradually increasing speed, then force; single-arm vortex at moderate intensity, short rounds Freestanding heavy bag; wraps, gloves for J-fist work 4+ weeks of moderate bag work with no symptoms; baseline tests stable (Appendix A)
4. Hard feedback (after 6+ months) Forearm and ulnar-border contact only, at first Alignment and rebound drills on the dummy: forearm, hammerfist, elbow contact, not full-force fist strikes Dummy arms padded with foam at first; bare steel only for light, controlled contact Months of pain-free padded work; no knuckle or wrist changes
5. Partners (Chapter 13) — Cooperative drills at agreed intensity, then graded resistance Gloves; headgear for any head contact Partner trust, control, and the rules in Chapter 11

These durations are minimums, not targets. If you are older, new to training, or have any history of hand injury, stay longer at each stage. If anything in a stage hurts, go back a stage.

Stop rules

  1. Sharp or localized pain in a knuckle, hand bone, wrist, or elbow, during or after striking.
  2. Swelling, bruising, or a knuckle that looks different, sits lower, or is tender to press. A depressed knuckle after a punch can mean a boxer’s fracture. Stop and get it examined.
  3. Pain on the little-finger side of the wrist, or a click or clunk in the wrist.
  4. Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the fingers, especially at night. Bent-wrist positions raise pressure in the carpal tunnel (Weiss et al., 1995).
  5. Pain that is worse the next morning than before you trained, or above about 3 out of 10 during training.
  6. Fatigue that degrades alignment. When the wrist starts to wobble at contact, the session is over.
  7. Any blow to your head or face, or any symptom of concussion in you or a partner: headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, blurred vision. Stop for the day and seek medical advice.
  8. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations, or faintness. Stop and seek medical attention.

If symptoms persist for more than a few days, or return every time you train, see a physician or hand therapist. Do not train through hand pain. Small hand injuries, ignored, become permanent ones.

Warm-up and session shape

Warming up improves performance in most studies (Fradkin et al., 2010), and for the hand it is also a daily check-in. A suggested session:

  1. Breath and check-in (2 min): slow, long-exhale breathing (Chapter 7). Open and close each hand slowly; press each knuckle; note anything new.
  2. Mobility (5 min): wrist circles, gentle flexion and extension, forearm rotation, shoulder circles, walking and turning (Book 1’s foundation).
  3. Slow wave (5 min): the whole-body wave in the air, then the micro-vortex very slowly on each side.
  4. Main work (10–20 min): the stage-appropriate work from the table, in short rounds of one to two minutes with rest between. Stop each round before form fades.
  5. Stop practice (2 min): run the micro-vortex and stop it on a cue at each station (Chapter 11).
  6. Cool-down (3 min): slow breathing; note how quickly heart rate settles; log the session (Appendix A).

Simple self-tests

Every four to six weeks, record the following. Use the same equipment, warm-up, and time of day each time, and remember that the first few tests mostly measure learning the test (Dunn et al., 2019).

  • Grip strength, neutral and flexed. With a hand dynamometer, record your best of three squeezes with the wrist in its natural position and again with the wrist held in your J-fist flexion. The ratio tells you how much clench the J posture costs you (O’Driscoll et al., 1992), and whether conditioning changes it.
  • Pain-free wrist range. Note the range of flexion and extension you can reach comfortably, and any pain.
  • Knuckle check. Look at and press each knuckle. Photograph your hands, flat and in a fist, from the same angle, each time.
  • Filmed micro-vortex. Record 10 seconds of the sequence on a bag, from the side, with a phone’s slow-motion mode, and count clean impacts and alignment at each contact (Chapter 13).

Train the hand for the decades, not the season.

How to Test It

Chapter 13

Full viability as a transmissible system requires progressive pressure-testing, filmed standards, and outcome data. — from the System of Inevitability source materials, May 2026

The System of Inevitability’s own materials say it plainly: to become more than a personal conditioning practice, it needs pressure-testing, filmed standards, and outcome data. The October 2026 viability assessment reached the same conclusion. This chapter is a practical guide to producing those things, honestly and safely, with equipment most people already own. It is offered in the spirit of the system’s own phrase: the tools, the physics, and the will to train, and, it might be added, the will to find out.

Why feelings and ratings are not enough

Every practitioner knows what it is like to feel that a technique works. That feeling is valuable; it is often how good ideas are discovered. But it is not evidence, for three well-documented reasons.

We overrate ourselves. In a famous series of studies, people who scored in the bottom quarter on tests of logic, grammar, and humour estimated their performance at around the 62nd percentile, when it was actually around the 12th. The skills needed to perform well are often the same skills needed to recognize good performance (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). A solitary practitioner, with no opponent and no teacher, is especially exposed to this.

Expectation changes performance. Placebo effects of varying size have been reported across sports, from weightlifting to endurance cycling, driven by expectation, motivation, and conditioning (Beedie & Foad, 2009). Someone who believes a technique is superior may genuinely perform it better, or rate it more highly, for reasons that have nothing to do with the technique.

Traditions can mislead their members. An anthropologist who has done fieldwork on martial arts since 2001, including seni silat, discusses an “infinity loop” model in which a practice’s real-world efficacy and its performance as display feed each other, and what happens when the two collide: misframing, captivation, and “false connections,” in which confounded variables give rise to new beliefs (Farrer, 2015).

The numerical ratings in the source conversation (9.6 out of 10 for the system, 9.1 compared with elite military close-quarters systems) belong in this category. They are impressions produced in a conversation with an AI system, not measurements. They could not be anything else, because no one has yet measured anything. The good news is that measuring is not hard.

● Evidence: well-established

Self-assessment is unreliable; expectation matters. People tend to overestimate their own competence, especially when less skilled (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). Expectations can produce placebo effects on sports performance (Beedie & Foad, 2009). This is why claims need external, repeatable measurement.

Five rules for a fair test

  1. State the claim precisely. “The J fist is superior” cannot be tested. “On a heavy bag, my J-fist straight strike moves the bag farther than my conventional straight punch, at the same effort” can.
  2. Compare with something. A number means little alone. Test the system’s technique against a conventional alternative, performed by the same person, on the same day, on the same target.
  3. Repeat. Single trials are noise. Measurement scientists recommend at least three trials when estimating reliability, and warn that systematic changes between trials, such as learning or fatigue, must be separated from random variation (Hopkins, 2000). In one boxing study, punch-force measurements became more consistent on the second testing day, suggesting a learning effect, and the authors recommended repeated familiarization (Dunn et al., 2019). Report the typical variation between your trials, not just your best one (Atkinson & Nevill, 1998).
  4. Blind what you can. Randomize the order of conditions. If someone else scores the videos, don’t tell them which condition they are watching.
  5. Write it down and share it, including the results you didn’t want.

The test kit

You do not need a laboratory to begin:

  • A phone with slow-motion video. An app using a phone’s high-speed video to time jump flight agreed almost perfectly with a laboratory force platform (Balsalobre-Fernández et al., 2015). Counting impacts and checking wrist alignment frame by frame is a simpler task.
  • A tripod or stack of books, so that every recording is from the same position.
  • A hand dynamometer for grip strength (Chapter 12).
  • A heart-rate monitor, if you have one.
  • Optionally, an accelerometer. Many phones and inexpensive sensors can record acceleration. A systematic review found inertial sensors increasingly used to measure strike quality in combat sports, but noted that methods are often ad hoc, so keep your method identical between sessions (Worsey et al., 2019).
  • Optionally, a striking dynamometer at a gym or university. Purpose-built devices can discriminate elite, intermediate, and novice punchers reliably (Smith et al., 2000), and reviews describe best practice for using them (Lenetsky et al., 2022).

Six solo tests

Test 1: Cadence. Claim: the micro-vortex produces 4–5 impacts in under a second. Film the single-arm sequence on a heavy bag from the side in slow motion. In editing software or frame by frame, count the impacts in each one-second window, and note which impacts were “clean” (wrist aligned, contact on the intended surface). Do five trials per arm. Report the average and range.

Test 2: Impact comparison. Claim: the J fist delivers more effective impacts than a conventional fist. With the same bag, distance, and stance, alternate in random order between conventional straight punches, J-fist straight strikes, and hammerfists, at the same perceived effort. Measure the bag’s swing on video (mark a scale on the wall behind it), or its peak acceleration with a sensor taped to the bag. Five to ten strikes per condition, repeated on three separate days. Record any pain for each condition.

Test 3: Grip cost. Question: how much clench does the J posture cost? Measure grip strength with the wrist neutral and in J-fist flexion (Chapter 12). The ratio is a simple, repeatable number that conditioning may or may not change.

Test 4: Alignment standard. Question: does structure hold at contact? Film the side view of each strike type at three speeds. Have a second person rate wrist and elbow alignment at the frame of contact on a simple five-point scale, a method like the one validated for police self-defence skills (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009). Two raters who agree are far more convincing than one.

Test 5: Economy. Claim: the system approaches “zero wasted motion.” For two-minute rounds, compare the micro-vortex with an ordinary punching combination that delivers the same number of impacts. Record heart rate and your rating of perceived effort at the end of each round. In fitness boxing, faster punching tempos raised heart rate and perceived effort (Kravitz et al., 2003); a genuinely more economical pattern should produce the same impacts at lower cost.

Test 6: The stop test. Question: can the sequence be interrupted? A partner or a phone app gives a random sound cue while you run the micro-vortex. Film it and count how many frames it takes to stop cleanly. This tests the restraint skill from Chapter 11, and it is as important as any test of power.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

These tests are suggestions. They are my designs, based on general measurement principles, not validated protocols. Their value lies in being simple, repeatable, filmed, and shared. If a qualified researcher wants to do better, so much the better.

Filmed standards

A belt system tells you that a teacher approved of you. A filmed standard tells everyone exactly what you can do. The system’s materials call for filmed standards, and they are a natural fit for a practice with “no instructors” and “no belts.”

A good standard has four parts:

  1. A defined task, such as “single-arm micro-vortex on a heavy bag, 30 seconds per arm.”
  2. Defined criteria, such as “at least 80% of contacts rated aligned by two raters; no visible wrist collapse; clean stop within a set number of frames on cue.”
  3. A fixed recording method: camera height, distance, angle, frame rate.
  4. Public, dated video, so that others can check and compare.

Standards like these could be the beginning of what the viability assessment called a “transmissible” system: not a hierarchy, but a shared, visible record of what the practice produces.

Partner pressure-testing: a ladder

Solo tests can answer questions about speed, alignment, and cost. They cannot answer the questions that matter most in a martial system: does it work against a person, and does it survive pressure? Chapters 9 and 10 explained why: expertise in fighting is perceptual and interactive (Krabben et al., 2019; Mori et al., 2002), solo practice differs from sparring (Kirk et al., 2015), and skill degrades under pressure unless it is trained under pressure (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009; Oudejans, 2008).

Here is a suggested ladder. Climb it slowly, with gloves, headgear for any head contact, a stop word, and the partner rules of Chapter 11.

  1. Cooperative. Partner holds pads or feeds a known, slow attack; you apply the technique. Goal: structure and timing with a moving person.
  2. Choice. Partner feeds one of two or three attacks at random. Goal: reading cues, not executing a plan.
  3. Constrained play. Light, flowing exchanges with limited targets (for example, body only, no head) and agreed intensity. Goal: adaptation against someone who also adapts.
  4. Graded resistance. Partner resists and counters at an agreed level that rises over weeks. Goal: does the method still function when the other person is trying to stop it?
  5. Scenarios. Realistic situations that begin before contact, with verbal de-escalation, avoidance, and the option, often the right one, of not striking at all. In a police study, training that rehearsed complete violent situations, including the moments before physical contact, improved officers’ performance in reality-based scenarios, with better communication, situational awareness, proportionality, and control (Renden et al., 2017). Goal: decisions under pressure.

At each rung, collect outcome data: how often the technique succeeds; independent ratings of video; and partners’ own reports. To test “psychological inevitability,” ask partners after each round, without telling them what you are testing, how predictable your movements felt on a simple scale. If the system makes you hard to read, it will show.

⚠ Caution

Pressure-testing is not permission to hurt people. The point is to raise unpredictability and psychological pressure, not to raise force. Never test on unconsenting people. Never test with full-force strikes to the head or neck. A test that injures a partner has failed, whatever else it showed.

Sharing the results

The final step is the one most often skipped. Share what you find, including the disappointing results, under an open license like this book’s. A dozen practitioners who each film and share their cadence, alignment, and comparison tests would, between them, create the first real data set on this system. A university biomechanics lab, offered a willing group of practitioners and a clear question, might do the rest.

That is how a personal practice becomes a contribution to human knowledge. It is also, in a quiet way, part of the upgrade this series hopes for: the willingness to put a cherished idea to the test, and to be glad of the answer, whatever it is.

The most inevitable thing about any idea is that, sooner or later, reality tests it. Better to do it yourself, kindly and carefully.

Wave and Return

Chapter 14

The cycle completes and restarts. — from the description of the micro-vortex

Make a fist. Not hard; just close your hand. Now let your wrist curl gently forward until the knuckles bow toward your forearm, into the shape this book has called the J fist. Feel the tendons on the back of your wrist lengthen, the little-finger edge of your hand line up with the bone of your forearm. Breathe out slowly.

Now open your hand.

That opening is where this book ends, and where, in a sense, every chapter has been pointing.

What we have learned

This book has tried to treat an unusual martial idea with both respect and honesty. Here is what the evidence supports:

  • A closed, buttressed fist protects the hand, and the structure of the hand, wrist, and forearm matters for how force is transmitted. Whether the System of Inevitability’s bent fist is better than a conventional fist is untested, and bent-wrist positions carry their own costs: weaker grip and higher carpal tunnel pressure.
  • Whole-body striking really is a wave. Skilled throws, kicks, and punches build speed from the ground up, segment by segment, and the ends of chains, like the tip of a whip, can move very fast. Elastic tissues store and return energy. These are real mechanics, and they are what lies behind the system’s language of waves, vortices, and flutter.
  • Loose, then firm, is how good strikers hit. Elite fighters relax during the strike and stiffen at contact. “Rock in a sock” is a vivid image of a well-documented pattern.
  • Figure-eights and rhythmic cycles are natural to the motor system, and continuous combinations are physically possible. Whether the micro-vortex delivers four or five effective impacts in under a second, on a resisting opponent, is something a phone camera can begin to answer.
  • Breath and calm can be trained, and slow breathing affects physiology and mood. Pressure degrades skill unless skill is trained under pressure.
  • Variation and perception are at the heart of skill. Never repeating the same strike twice has support in motor-learning research. But fighting skill lives in the interaction with another person, which solo training alone cannot supply.
  • Martial arts do not automatically make people better or worse. What matters is how they are taught and practised: with restraint, respect, and a culture of care.

And here is what remains open: the bent fist’s superiority, the system’s economy, its effectiveness against resisting partners, and its “psychological inevitability.” Those are not weaknesses of the book or of the system. They are its research programme.

The real return

Every strike in the micro-vortex flows back into the next. That is its beauty, and its danger: a cycle designed never to stop.

The most important skill this book can offer is the opposite: the return to stillness. The capacity to stop on a cue. To feel the wave rising in your body, in anger or fear, and let it settle. To walk away from a fight that does not need to happen, which is almost every fight. To open the hand.

Research on de-escalation and violence prevention points to the same lesson from every direction. The safest confrontation is the one that never escalates; the strongest person in the room is often the calmest; and the training that best prepares people for violence includes, at its centre, the words and choices that come before it.

If there is an “upgrade in human consciousness” to be found in a practice of striking, it is this: to hold real power in your hands and to become, because of it, more patient, more careful, and more kind. To be able to hurt and to choose not to. To train hard and come home whole. To help a training partner improve without injuring them. To test your beliefs and be glad to learn you were wrong.

An invitation

Train patiently. Follow the safe path. Bone and tendon keep their own calendar.

Measure honestly. Film your standards. Count your impacts. Compare. Share what you find, including what disappoints you.

Train with others. Find partners you trust, and become a partner others can trust.

Practise stopping. Every session, rehearse the most important technique in this book: the moment you choose not to strike.

Share freely. This book belongs to everyone who reads it. Give it away. Improve it. Pass it on.

The wave goes out. The wave returns.

Let what returns be gentler than what went out.

— with gratitude for the practice and the questions it raises; to the researchers whose work is cited here, for the evidence; and to every training partner who has ever pulled a strike, for the care.

Appendix A · Test Protocols and Logs

Copy or print these pages. Fill them in honestly. Film what you can. Over time, your logs and videos will tell you more than any rating ever could.

Filming checklist

  • Same camera position every time: tripod or fixed stack, at hip height, 2–3 m from the bag, side-on (90°) to the line of the strike.
  • Slow-motion mode (120 fps or higher if available); good light; plain background.
  • Mark a scale on the wall behind the bag (tape marks every 10 cm) for swing measurements.
  • Say the date, test, and condition aloud at the start of each clip.
  • Randomize the order of conditions (write them on cards and shuffle).
  • Keep every clip, including the bad ones.

Self-test log (every 4–6 weeks)

Grip in kg, best of three. Impacts per second: average of five filmed one-second windows (Test 1).

Date Grip neutral L/R Grip J L/R Wrist pain-free? Knuckles OK? Impacts per s Clean % Stop (frames) Notes

Fist comparison log (Test 2)

Record bag swing (cm, from the wall scale) or peak acceleration, five trials per condition, in shuffled order.

Date Order Conventional J fist Hammerfist Effort (1–10) Pain (0–10) Blind?

Economy log (Test 5)

Date Pattern Round length Impacts delivered Heart rate at end Effort (1–10) Heart rate 1 min after Notes
Micro-vortex 2 min
Conventional combination 2 min
Micro-vortex 2 min
Conventional combination 2 min

Partner pressure-testing log

Date Partner Rung (1–5) Intensity Success / tries Predictable? (1–5) Injury? What I learned

Session and injury log

Appendix B · The Evidence at a Glance

A one-page summary of the main claims discussed in this book, how strong the evidence is, and where to look. “●” marks well-established findings, “◐” suggestive or emerging ones, and “○” practitioner claims that have not been tested.

Claim Strength Key sources
A tightly buttressed fist stiffens the knuckles and reduces strain on hand bones ◐ Suggestive (small lab studies; interpretation debated) Morgan & Carrier, 2013; Horns et al., 2015; Nickle & Goncharoff, 2013
Grip strength drops and carpal-tunnel pressure rises as the wrist bends away from neutral ● Well-established O’Driscoll et al., 1992; Weiss et al., 1995
Hand and wrist injuries are the most common injuries in boxing; protection reduces risk ● Well-established Loosemore et al., 2015, 2017; Diesselhorst et al., 2013; Drury et al., 2017
The J fist is structurally superior to the straight fist ○ Untested System materials
Skilled striking sequences body segments proximal to distal (a “wave”) ● Well-established Putnam, 1993; Hirashima et al., 2007; Marshall & Elliott, 2000
Tendons store and return elastic energy; the stretch-shortening cycle boosts power ● Well-established Roberts & Azizi, 2011; Komi, 2000; Roach et al., 2013
“Toroidal energy fields,” “butterfly-flutter resonance,” “fractal chaining” ○ Metaphor System materials
Elite strikers relax mid-strike and stiffen at impact (double peak) ◐ Suggestive (one small study) McGill et al., 2010
Effective mass and speed both determine impact; trained strikers couple more mass ● Well-established Neto et al., 2007; Walilko et al., 2005; Lenetsky et al., 2015
“100% energy economy” / “zero wasted motion” ○ Untested (physically impossible as stated) System materials
Coordination patterns self-organize and switch abruptly ● Well-established Haken et al., 1985; Kelso & Schöner, 1988
Practised sequences become chunks ● Well-established (general finding) Sakai et al., 2003; Wymbs et al., 2012
4–5 impacts in under a second, with compounding resonance ○ Untested (cadence plausible; resonance unsupported) System materials
Shouting or grunting slightly boosts force ◐ Suggestive Welch & Tschampl, 2012; O’Connell et al., 2014
Slow breathing reduces arousal and improves mood ● Well-established for HRV; ◐ for mood Zaccaro et al., 2018; Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014; Balban et al., 2023
Systema breath principles and military use ○ Not studied; military claims unverified —
Variable or random practice improves retention and transfer ● Well-established Shea & Morgan, 1979; Hall & Magill, 1995; Wu et al., 2014
Highly variable “differential learning” ◐ Promising but debated Tassignon et al., 2021; Schöllhorn et al., 2022
Expert fighters anticipate from early cues ● Well-established Mori et al., 2002; Mann et al., 2007; Milazzo et al., 2016
Solo practice differs from live practice; transfer is specific ● Well-established Kirk et al., 2015; Sala & Gobet, 2017; Pinder et al., 2011
“Psychological inevitability” ○ Untested System materials
Pressure degrades skill; training under pressure protects it ● Well-established Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009; Oudejans & Pijpers, 2009; Nieuwenhuys & Oudejans, 2011
Mindfulness protects attention under stress ◐ Suggestive Jha et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2014
Single blows to the head can kill ● Well-established Pilgrim et al., 2014
Martial arts improve wellbeing and reduce aggression ◐ Mixed: depends on teaching and culture Moore et al., 2020; Harwood et al., 2017; Gubbels et al., 2016
De-escalation training reduces force and injuries ◐ Promising (one strong trial) Engel et al., 2022; Engel et al., 2020
Bone and tendon adapt to gradual loading over months; load spikes raise injury risk ● Well-established Warden et al., 2014; Bohm et al., 2015; Gabbett, 2016
People overrate their own competence; expectation affects performance ● Well-established Kruger & Dunning, 1999; Beedie & Foad, 2009

Glossary

Angular velocity — How fast something rotates, measured in degrees or radians per second. The speed of a fist depends on the angular velocities of the segments behind it.

Boxer’s fracture — A break in the neck of a metacarpal bone, usually the fourth or fifth, often caused by striking a hard object with a closed fist.

Buttressed fist — A fist in which the thumb wraps across the fingers, stiffening the knuckle joints so that the hand behaves more like a single rigid unit at impact.

Carpal tunnel — The passage on the palm side of the wrist through which the median nerve and finger flexor tendons run. Pressure in it rises when the wrist is strongly bent.

Chunking — The brain’s grouping of a practised sequence of movements into units executed as wholes.

Constraints-led approach — A way of teaching skills by designing the task, environment, and rules so that good solutions emerge, rather than prescribing a single correct technique.

De-escalation — Words, posture, distance, and choices that reduce the intensity of a conflict and the likelihood of violence.

Differential learning — A practice method that deliberately adds large, constant variation, so that no movement is repeated exactly.

Double peak — The pattern of muscle activation seen in elite strikers: an initial burst, a period of relative relaxation as the limb accelerates, and a second burst at impact.

Effective mass — The amount of body mass that behaves as though it were rigidly coupled to the striking surface at the moment of impact.

Figure-eight (lemniscate) — A closed curve that crosses itself once, like the symbol ∞. In this book, a description of the paths of the hands and elbows in continuous striking.

Filmed standard — A defined task, criteria, and recording method, with dated public video, used to show what a practitioner can actually do.

Hammerfist — A strike with the little-finger edge of the closed fist.

HKB model — The Haken–Kelso–Bunz model of coordination, which describes how rhythmic movements settle into stable patterns and switch abruptly between them.

Impulse — Force multiplied by the time over which it acts; equal to the change in momentum it produces.

J fist (bent fist, Monyet hand) — In the System of Inevitability, a clenched fist with the wrist bent sharply toward the palm, so that the knuckles, little-finger edge, forearm, and elbow form a continuous striking surface. The name “Monyet hand” (tangan monyet, “monkey hand”) comes from silat.

Kinetic chain — The linked sequence of body segments that transfers energy from the ground to the hand or foot.

Metacarpals — The five long bones of the hand between the wrist and the fingers. Their heads form the knuckles.

Micro-vortex — The System of Inevitability’s single-arm sequence: bent-fist punch, same-spot elbow, backwards hammerfist, lateral elbow, and return to the punch.

Momentum — Mass multiplied by velocity. The quantity transferred to a target in an impact.

Placebo effect — A change in performance or symptoms caused by expectation rather than by the specific treatment or technique.

Representative design — Designing practice so that it preserves the key information of the real situation, such as a live, responsive opponent.

“Rock in a sock” — The System of Inevitability’s image for a relaxed, whip-like arm that locks into structure only at impact.

Silat (pencak silat) — A family of martial arts from the Malay archipelago, including Indonesia and Malaysia.

Stretch-shortening cycle — A muscle-tendon action in which a quick stretch is immediately followed by a shortening, increasing force and power through stored elastic energy and reflexes.

Systema — A Russian martial art emphasizing breathing, relaxation, and continuous movement. Little peer-reviewed research exists on it.

Toroidal — Shaped like a torus (a doughnut). In this book, a metaphor for circulating paths of movement, not a physical energy field.

Typical error — The standard deviation of a person’s repeated measurements on the same test; a simple measure of how much a result varies by chance.

Ulnar border — The little-finger edge of the hand and forearm, along the ulna bone.

About This Book

Title. Wave and Return: The Bent Fist, the Figure-Eight, and the Science of a Restrained Hand. Book 2 of the Companions to the System of Inevitability.

Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. First edition, November 2026.

Also in this series. Book 1: Walking and Turning: Iron, Spirals, and the Science of a Practicing Mind, on the iron balls, the ring bar, and the brain science of juggling and skill. Book 3: Shape and Choice: Everyday Geometry, Calm Presence, and the Science of a Choosing Mind, on the system’s everyday geometry, solitary training, calm presence, my own list of dangers, and the science of keeping choice inside automatic skill. Book 4: Lens and Lattice: Altered Perception, the Internal Arts, and the Science of a Curious Practice, a harm-reduction companion on practising the internal arts with curiosity in altered states, responsibly, and on the science of psilocybin, perception, touch, pattern finding, and integration. Book 5: Nucleus and Orbit: Atoms, Necessity, and the Science of an Interwoven Practice, on the system’s atomism, its 3-6-9 architecture, and its quantum language set beside the real science of atoms, necessity, chaos, the fractal body, and interdependence, tying the series together. The series continues.

About this book. Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. Descriptions of the System are based on a consolidation of a May 2026 conversation about the system and on a separate viability assessment (October 2026). All progressions, tests, stop rules, and ethical guidance in this book are mine, drawn from general exercise, motor-learning, and violence-prevention science.

Method. Every peer-reviewed study cited was checked against its Crossref record (authors, year, title, journal, volume, pages, DOI), and the specific findings reported were checked against the published abstracts or full texts. Numbers are reported as the original authors reported them. Where a claim is untested, the text says so. No quotations have been invented. Numerical ratings that appear in the source conversation are reported once, as impressions from an AI conversation, and are not treated as evidence.

Illustrations. All diagrams are original schematics created for this book. Diagrams marked illustrative show shapes, not data. No figure depicts any real person.

Typography. Set in EB Garamond and Cormorant Garamond, with Inter for labels.

Not advice. Nothing in this book is medical or legal advice. Laws on self-defence and the use of force differ between countries and states.

Corrections. Science moves. If you find an error, or a new study that bears on anything here, please share it, and share a corrected copy under the same license.
